insurance claims an insurer successfully pays out against the total claims received in a financial year. It is an essential value used to determine how reliable an insurer is and track their performance record. If an insurance company has a high CSR, it means the insurer has a strong track record of fulfilling claims and processing them efficiently. As an industry standard, a CSR above 90% is viewed as excellent, and anything above 85% is strong. A mediclaim claim settlement ratio (CSR) is the percentage of total claims an insurer successfully approves against the total number of claims filed within a financial year. Before buying health insurance , most people focus on the premium, coverage amount, and benefits. However, one factor that often makes the biggest difference during a medical emergency is the Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR). A health insurance claim settlement ratio shows how reliably and efficiently an insurance company pays the claims it receives. A higher ratio generally indicates that the insurer settles a larger percentage of claims, making it a vital factor to consider before choosing a policy. The real value of health insurance can be determined only when you need to make a claim. This article explains the meaning of claim settlement ratio, its formula, what is considered a good ratio, CSR vs ICR, how to check it, and a comparison of insurers. What is the Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR) in health insurance? A health insurance claim settlement ratio is one of the most important indicators of an insurance company’s reliability. It highlights the percentage of claims an insurance company settles out of the total claims it receives during a financial year. For example, if an insurance company receives 1,000 claim requests and settles 970 of them, its CSR is 97%. Such a high claim settlement ratio generally suggests that the insurer handles and pays claims more efficiently. Health insurance buyers must consider this factor when comparing health insurance companies to make a wise insurance investment. Read More – Individual or Corporate Health Insurance How is the claim settlement ratio calculated? The health insurance claim settlement ratio is calculated using the simple formula given below: CSR = (Total Claims Settled / Total Claims Received) X 100 This formula shows the percentage of claims an insurer has successfully settled during a financial year. Let’s understand this with the help of an example. Suppose ABC insurance company receives 10,000 health insurance claims in a particular financial year. The company settles 9500 of them successfully and processes the claim amounts. The CSR will be calculated as follows: CSR = (9500 / 10000) X 100 = 95% This means the insurer settled 95 out of every 100 claims received. Generally, a higher CSR indicates better claim-settlement performance and reliability. Read More – Group health insurance What is a good claim settlement ratio? Insurance regulators haven’t prescribed a fixed claim settlement ratio as a benchmark. However, as an industry standard, a CSR above 85% is considered good, while a ratio above 90% is often viewed as excellent. A higher medical insurance claim settlement ratio suggests that the insurer settles most of the claims it receives. While comparing health insurance companies using CSR, do not rely on a single year’s figure itself. Evaluate the insurer’s CSR trend over the last three years and compare similar insurers to get a more accurate picture of claim-settlement performance. CSR vs Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR): What’s the difference? Many people confuse the Claim Settlement Ratio (CSR) with the Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR). However, they measure different things. CSR assesses the number of claims settled. On the other hand, ICR looks at the amount of money paid out in claims compared to premiums collected. The following table highlights the differences between CSR and ICR. Factor CSR ICR Meaning Claims settled / Claims received Claims paid / Premiums earned Measures Claim handling efficiency Financial performance Is a higher ratio better? Generally, yes Ideally around 70% to 90% Concern A low CSR may indicate more claim rejections A very low ICR may suggest restrictive practices; a very high ICR may indicate financial stress You must consider both CSR and ICR together when evaluating health insurance. Also Read – Health insurance claim process Why does a claim settlement ratio matter when buying health insurance? A claim settlement ratio matters while buying health insurance because it helps you judge how reliable an insurer may be when you need to make a claim. Here are some other reasons why it’s important: Shows claim-settlement track record: A higher CSR generally means more claims are being settled. Indicates fewer claim hassles: If the CSR meets industry standards, it reflects smoother claim handling. Helps compare insurers: You can use the metric to shortlist health insurance plans. However, CSR is one signal among several. You must not review it alone. Make sure you also check the insurer’s ICR, complaint ratio, network hospitals, and claim turnaround time to get a complete picture and make a better insurance decision. How to check an insurer’s claim settlement ratio? You can check an insurer’s claim settlement ratio by following the steps mentioned below: Visit the insurer’s official website and look for annual reports, investor presentations, or claim-related disclosures. Check reputable insurance comparison and aggregator websites that compile CSR data. Refer to IRDAI reports for the insurer’s Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR), which is published more prominently than CSR. Compare figures from multiple sources for accuracy. Always note the financial year of the data, as claim performance can change from year to year. Review at least the last 3 years of available data. What is the claim settlement ratio of health insurers in India (Latest data)? The latest health insurance claim ratio in India for different insurers, as released by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), is as follows: Insurer Claims paid within 3 months (%) Aditya Birla Health Insurance 100.00% Galaxy Health Insurance 100.00% Narayana Health Insurance 100.00% Niva Bupa Health Insurance 100.00% Care Health Insurance 99.95% ManipalCigna Health Insurance 99.88% Star Health & Allied Insurance 99.81% Source: IRDAI Handbook of Indian Insurance Statistics, FY 2024-25, reported in February 2026. [1] The figures represent the percentage of claims paid within three months and should not be confused with the Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR) or insurer-advertised Claim Settlement Ratios. Note: This section must be refreshed annually after the latest IRDAI annual disclosures and insurer reports become available. Also Read – Personal loan for medical emergencies vs health insurance Beyond CSR: What are the IRDAI turnaround time (TAT) rules? It is important for an insurer to have a high claim settlement ratio, but it does not reflect the entire picture. The speed at which an insurer processes and settles claims is equally important. Under the IRDAI Master Circular on Health Insurance (29 May 2024), insurers must meet specific claim-processing timelines, making service quality another key factor to evaluate. Cashless pre-authorization: It must be processed within 1 hour of receiving the request. Final cashless authorization: It must be issued within 3 hours of the hospital’s discharge request. Reimbursement claims: These claims must generally be settled within 30 days of receiving all required documents. Today, when you compare insurers, claim service speed complements CSR. Which factors should be considered along with the claim settlement ratio? When you are choosing a health insurance plan, checking the health insurance claim settlement ratio is important. But there are other factors, too, that you should consider. These include: Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR): It shows the insurer’s claim-paying performance against the premiums collected. Grievance or complaint ratio: It indicates customer satisfaction and service quality. Network hospital list: If an insurer has a larger network of hospitals, you have access to more treatment options. Cashless claim availability: This feature makes hospitalization smoother and reduces out-of-pocket expenses. Waiting periods: Generally, it is better to have shorter waiting periods. Claim process ease: The insurer must offer a simple and quick claim procedure to improve the overall experience. Conclusion A medical insurance claim settlement ratio is a useful indicator of how reliably an insurer handles claims. However, it should not be viewed in isolation. You must review the insurer’s performance over multiple years, instead of focusing on a single year’s numbers. You must compare it with other important factors such as the Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR), complaint levels, network hospitals, and claim turnaround times. These metrics together provide a clearer picture of an insurer’s service quality. Before buying a policy, you must verify the latest figures from official insurer disclosures and regulatory sources. There is no official benchmark for a good health insurance claim settlement ratio. But a ratio above 85% is generally considered good, and a ratio over 90% is often seen as excellent. You must always review the insurer’s performance over several years rather than relying on a single year’s figure to make an informed decision. What is the difference between CSR and the incurred claim ratio? CSR measures the percentage of claims settled out of claims received. On the other hand, the Incurred Claims Ratio (ICR) measures the value of claims paid compared to premiums earned. CSR reflects claim-handling efficiency, while ICR indicates the insurer’s overall claims-paying experience and financial balance. How is the health insurance claim settlement ratio calculated? The formula for calculating the health insurance claim ratio is: (Total claims settled / total claims received) X 100 So, if a company settles 960 claims out of the 1,000 claims received, it has a CSR of 96%. Where can I check an insurer’s claim settlement ratio? You can check an insurer’s health insurance claim ratio on its official website, annual reports, product disclosures, and reputable insurance comparison websites. The ICR data is available on IRDAI publications. Always check the financial year to ensure the information is current. Is a higher claim settlement ratio always better? If an insurer has a higher CSR, it is generally positive because it suggests that the company is settling more claims. However, you must not consider CSR only. You must also review ICR, complaint levels, hospital network size, cashless facilities, and claim settlement timelines. Does CSR guarantee my claim will be approved? No. CSR is a percentage of how many claims the insurer approves against the claims it receives. For approval, your claim must meet the policy terms, coverage conditions, waiting periods, exclusions, and documentation requirements specified in the health insurance policy. What claim settlement timelines does IRDAI mandate? Under IRDAI’s health insurance guidelines, an insurer must process cashless pre-authorization within 1 hour and final cashless authorization within 3 hours of the discharge request. Generally, reimbursement claims are to be settled within 30 days. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund The Goods and Services Tax (GST) for health insurance is an indirect tax levied on your medical insurance premium. Prior to 22 September, 2025, GST was charged at 18% on health insurance premiums, making policies costlier. However, following recent tax reforms, individual health policies and family floater plans are fully exempt, meaning 0% GST is charged on them, whereas employer-issued group/corporate policies still attract an 18% GST. The additional taxes are added to the total premium your employer pays for the health policies. GST on health insurance premiums is exempt for individual policies, while group and corporate health insurance plans continue to attract 18% GST. If you are a new or existing health insurance policyholder, you must know about the recent developments related to Goods and Services Tax (GST) in health insurance . Since 22 September 2025, individual health insurance policies in India are GST-free. This means no GST is charged on the premium. However, group health insurance plans provided by corporate entities or employers continue to attract 18% GST. This change has made health insurance more affordable for many individuals and families. Through this article, you can learn about the current applicable GST on health insurance premiums in India, how to calculate the tax, and much more. What is GST on health insurance? GST on health insurance premiums is an indirect tax levied by the government on the insurance service (HSN 997133) provided by insurers. For several years, an 18% GST applied to health insurance premiums, which increased the overall cost of coverage. However, GST rules were changed in September 2025, and the tax treatment now depends on the type of health insurance policy you have. Read on to learn about the revised health insurance GST rate. Also Read – GST on rent in India What is the current GST rate on health insurance (2025 update)? According to the 2025 update, the type of policy determines how much GST is charged on health insurance premiums. No GST applies to individual health insurance plans. This includes family floater and senior citizen policies. However, there is an 18% GST charge on group or corporate health insurance plans. The following table explains the health insurance GST rate as per the 2025 update: Type of health insurance policy GST rate Individual health insurance Nil (Exempt) Family floater health insurance Nil (Exempt) Senior citizen health insurance Nil (Exempt) Group/corporate health insurance 18% What is the GST on individual health insurance? The government of India amended the GST rules on health insurance in September 2025. Since then, individual health insurance policies have been GST-exempt. This exemption includes individual plans, family floater policies, senior citizen health insurance, and individual top-up or super top-up plans. It applies to premiums paid on or after this date. It also includes renewals and reinstated policies. Moreover, reinsurance services related to these exempt individual health insurance policies are also GST-free. Read More – Input Tax Credit (ITC) under GST What is the GST on group/corporate health insurance? Despite the 2025 update, group and corporate health insurance policies provided by employers continue to attract GST at 18%. This means GST is added to the premium paid for employee health coverage. It is vital for businesses to note that Input Tax Credit (ITC) on employee health insurance is generally blocked under Section 17(5)(b) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act. However, you may get ITC if providing such health cover is mandatory under any applicable law. Read More – Which is recommended, individual or corporate health insurance The September 2025 GST exemption: What changed? In September 2025, a major change came into effect when the GST Council reduced GST on individual health and life insurance from 18% to nil. The decision was made at the 56th GST Council meeting on 3 September 2025, and came into effect from 22 September 2025 through Notification No. 16/2025-CT(R). The key changes include: Removing GST from individual health insurance premiums Making individual life insurance premiums GST-free The amended GST for health insurance approach focused on supporting the “Insurance for All by 2047” vision. As a result, premiums are now lower because of no GST addition. How to calculate GST on a health insurance premium? The GST is nil for individual health insurance policies issued, renewed, or reinstated on or after 22 September 2025. This means that you only pay the base premium amount. The formula is: Base premium = Payable amount For example, if an individual policy’s premium is Rs. 15,000, you will pay Rs. 15,000 to the insurance company. For group health insurance plans, add GST at 18% to the premium amount. The formula is: Total payable = Premium + 18% of the premium as GST So, if the premium for a group health insurance plan is Rs. 20,000, you will pay Rs. 3,600 (20,000 X 18%) as GST. So, the total payable will be Rs. 23,600 (20,000 + 3,600). Read More – How to calculate GST on a home loan What is a GST calculation example? As clarified above, GST calculation depends on the type of health insurance policy. In the following example, the premium for both individual and group health insurance policies is the same, but GST applicability is different. As a result, the total payable amount is also different. Policy type Premium GST Total payable Individual health insurance Rs. 50,000 Nil Rs. 50,000 Group health insurance Rs. 50,000 Rs. 9,000 Rs. 59,000 Which premiums are exempt? Transition and timing rules The applicability of GST on health insurance premiums depends on the timing rules specified under Section 14 of the CGST Act. These rules focus on when the supply is made, when the invoice is issued, and when the payment is received. Therefore, the date of premium payment is vital in determining whether GST applies. Individual health premiums paid on or after 22 September 2025: No GST applies to new policy premiums. No GST applies to renewal premiums. Installment premiums are GST-exempt. No GST applies to premiums paid for reinstated policies. Individual health insurance premiums paid before 22 September 2025: GST applies at 18% What are the GST exemption and Section 80D tax benefits? The GST exemption on individual health insurance and the tax deduction available under Section 80D are two separate benefits. You can continue to claim Section 80D deductions on eligible health insurance premiums as long as they are available in your tax regime and within prescribed limits. On the other hand, since no GST is charged on individual health insurance premiums paid on or after 22 September 2025, the amount you pay and potentially claim as a deduction is lower than before. Note that tax rules vary based on your situation. You must consult a qualified tax advisor or financial professional before making tax-related decisions. Read More – What Is GST on Personal Loan What is the impact of the GST exemption on policyholders? Individual health insurance has become more affordable with GST exemption, as it reduces the total premium payable on new policies and renewals. Since there is no GST in health insurance, individuals and families can save money while maintaining the same level of coverage. However, group and corporate health insurance policies continue to attract 18% GST. Thus, there is no change for employer-sponsored plans. If you receive an insurance renewal notice after 22 September 2025, make sure you review it carefully to ensure the GST exemption has been applied correctly. Conclusion GST for health insurance is an indirect tax that the government charges for the services an insurance company provides to you. However, its applicability has changed significantly after the GST Council meeting held on 3 September 2025. Earlier, insurance premiums attracted an 18% GST. But, effective 22 September 2025, GST charges depend on the type of policy. Individual and family floater insurance plans are GST-exempt, whereas 18% GST still applies to group/corporate health insurance plans. You must always check the latest GST rates and policy details through official GST notifications, government portals, or your insurer, as these can change from time to time. Popular Searches group medical insurance for employees FAQs How much GST is charged on health insurance now? The health insurance GST rate depends on the policy type. Individual health insurance policies are exempt from GST. However, group and corporate health insurance policies continue to attract GST at 18% on the premium amount. Is GST applicable to individual health insurance in 2026? No, GST does not apply to individual health insurance, including family floater and senior citizen plans, in 2026. This means no GST is charged on eligible individual health insurance premiums as long as the GST Council doesn’t make changes to the exemption. Do group health insurance policies still attract GST? Yes, group health insurance policies provided by employers or organizations still attract GST. The rate is set at 18%. It is added to the premium amount payable for the group insurance cover. When is health insurance GST-exempt? Individual health insurance is GST-exempt from 22 September 2025. The decision was made via Notification No. 16/2025-CT(R) in the GST Council meeting held on 3 September 2025. The exemption applies to eligible premiums paid on or after this date, including new policies, renewals, installments, and reinstated policies. Are renewal premiums exempt from GST? Yes. Renewal premiums for eligible individual health insurance policies are exempt from GST if they are paid on or after 22 September 2025. However, if the premiums are paid before that date, they continue to attract 18% GST as per the earlier GST rules. How do I calculate GST on a group health insurance premium? The GST on medical insurance premiums for group plans is calculated at 18% of the premium amount. So, if the group medical insurance premium is Rs. 1,00,000, the GST is Rs. 18,000 (1,00,000 X 18%), and the total amount payable is Rs. 1,18,000 (1,00,000 + 18,000). Does the GST exemption affect my Section 80D deduction? No, the GST exemption has no impact on your Section 80D deduction. They are separate benefits. You can continue claiming Section 80D deductions as per the application conditions, tax regime, and deduction limits. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund A finance lease is a long-term financial arrangement that allows businesses to use expensive assets without purchasing them outright. It is commonly used for machinery, vehicles, equipment, and technology assets. While the lessor retains legal ownership, the lessee assumes most of the risks and rewards associated with the asset. Financial leases help preserve working capital and spread costs over time, but they also involve long-term payment commitments and balance-sheet obligations. Understanding the features, types, benefits, and limitations of finance leases can help businesses c hoose the right financing option . A finance lease is a long-term lease in which a business uses an asset for most of its useful life while making regular payments and assuming most ownership-related risks and rewards. Rohit had recently started a small manufacturing business and wanted to purchase advanced machinery to increase production. The problem was that the equipment was expensive, and buying it outright would have put a significant strain on his working capital . While discussing the issue with a friend, he came across the concept of a financial lease. Instead of paying the full cost upfront, Rohit could use the equipment by making periodic lease payments over an agreed period. This allowed him to access the assets his business needed without a large initial investment. Many businesses face a similar challenge when they need costly equipment, vehicles, or machinery but do not want to tie up a large amount of capital. A financial lease offers a practical solution by spreading the cost over time while allowing the business to use the asset. In this guide, we explain the finance lease meaning, its key features, types, advantages, disadvantages, examples, and how it differs from other forms of leasing. What is a finance lease? A finance lease is a long-term arrangement in which a business or individual obtains the right to use an asset for most of its useful life in exchange for regular lease payments. In this arrangement, the lessor (owner of the asset) retains legal ownership, but the lessee (user of the asset) assumes most of the risks and rewards associated with ownership, including maintenance, insurance , and obsolescence risk. Financial leases are commonly used for expensive assets such as machinery, equipment, vehicles, and industrial plants. They allow businesses to use essential assets without making a large upfront purchase. Read More – Commercial Vehicle Lease What is the leasing definition in finance? In finance, leasing is a method of using an asset without purchasing it outright. Under a lease agreement, the lessor owns the asset and grants the lessee the right to use it for a specified period in return for regular payments. Leasing in financial services is often used to finance heavy equipment, vehicles, machinery, and other assets. It helps businesses conserve capital, offers flexibility, and may also include maintenance or service arrangements depending on the terms of the lease. Also Read – Working Capital: Meaning, Formula and Importance How does a finance lease work? Now that you have understood what a finance lease is, let’s discuss how it works in practice. The process is fairly simple and can be explained through the following steps: Step 1 – Asset selection The financial lease process begins with the lessee identifying the equipment, machinery, vehicle, or other asset required for business use. Step 2 – Lessor purchases the asset Once the lessor learns of the requirement, it purchases the required asset(s) from the supplier and becomes the legal owner. Step 3 – Preparation of a lease agreement Both parties sign a lease contract that specifies the lease term, payment schedule, maintenance responsibilities, and end-of-lease conditions. Step 4 – Periodic lease payments The lessee uses the asset and makes regular lease payments. Step 5 – End-of-term options Once the lease period ends, the lessee may choose to return the asset, renew the lease, or purchase it at a pre-agreed price. Read More – Project Finance in India: Definition, Types, & Benefits What are the key features of a finance lease? Some of the key features of a finance lease include: Long lease term : The lease period is usually enough to cover the asset’s useful life. Transfer of risks/rewards : The lessor remains the legal owner of the asset. However, the lessee assumes most of the risks and benefits associated with using the asset. Non-cancelable contract : Financial leases are usually non-cancelable. It means the lessee cannot terminate the contract or refuse to make lease payments during the term of the lease. Purchase/bargain option: Many finance leases provide the lessee with an option to buy the asset at the end of the lease at a bargain price. Lessee bears maintenance: The lessee is typically responsible for maintenance, repairs, insurance and other operating costs associated with the asset. On-balance-sheet treatment: Finance lease assets and related liabilities are generally recorded on the lessee’s balance sheet. Also Read – Types of Working Capital: Policies & Financing Options What are the components of a finance lease agreement? A financial lease agreement typically contains the following details: Lessor and lessee details : Names and information of both parties. Asset description : Details of the equipment, vehicle, machinery, or other asset being leased. Asset cost : Purchase value of the leased asset. Economic life : Expected useful life of the asset. Interest or lease rate : Charges applicable to the lease. Payment schedule : Amount and frequency of lease payments. Penalties and fees : Charges for late payments, defaults, or other contractual breaches. What are the different types of leases in finance? The leasing definition in finance encompasses several types of arrangements designed to meet different business and financing needs. Leases are usually classified based on factors such as the lease term, ownership rights, transfer of risks and rewards, and the responsibilities of the lessor and lessee. Understanding these categories is important because each type offers a different balance of flexibility, cost, and ownership benefits. Here are the four common types of leases in finance: Finance (Capital) lease A finance lease or capital lease is a long-term arrangement in which the lessee uses the asset for most of its useful life. While the lessor retains legal ownership, most risks and rewards associated with the asset are transferred to the lessee. In many cases, the lease includes an option to purchase the asset at a pre-agreed or bargained-for price. Operating lease An operating lease is usually used when an asset is needed only for a limited period. The lessee pays to use the asset and returns it at the end of the lease. Ownership and risk/reward stay with the lessor throughout the arrangement. This type of lease is common for assets that may need frequent replacement, such as office equipment, computers, or company vehicles. Sale and leaseback In a sale and leaseback transaction, a company first sells an asset it owns and then takes it back on lease from the buyer. This helps the company raise funds from the sale while continuing to use the asset for its day-to-day operations. Businesses often use this option when they need additional cash without giving up access to important assets. Leveraged lease A leveraged lease is generally used for expensive assets. In this arrangement, the lessor does not provide the full amount required to purchase the asset. Instead, a lender finances a portion of the purchase cost. As a result, three parties are involved – the lessor, the lessee, and the lender. Such leases are commonly seen in sectors that use high-value equipment and infrastructure. Read More – Equipment Lease Financing vs Equipment Loan Finance lease vs operating lease Both finance leases and operating leases allow businesses to use assets without purchasing them outright. However, they differ significantly in terms of ownership benefits, risk allocation, and lease duration. The table below compares the two types of leases: Basis Financial Lease Operating Lease Asset ownership Legal ownership remains with the lessor. The lessor is the legal owner of the asset(s). Term length Usually long enough to cover the asset’s useful life. Shorter than the asset’s life. Risk/reward Usually transferred to the lessee. Usually retained by the lessor. Cancelability Usually non-cancelable during the lease term. Often more flexible and may allow cancellation under certain conditions. Balance-sheet treatment Typically recognized as an asset and liability on the lessee’s balance sheet. Historically treated as off-balance-sheet. Suitable for Businesses that need long-term use of an asset. Businesses seeking flexibility or short-term access to an asset. What are the advantages and disadvantages of a finance lease? A financial lease can be a useful tool for businesses that need expensive assets but do not want to make a large upfront investment. However, like any other financing arrangement, it comes with both benefits and drawbacks. Understanding these pros and cons can help businesses decide whether a finance lease is the right option for their needs. Advantages of a finance lease: No large upfront capital investment is required. Businesses can get access to costly equipment or infrastructure. Preserves working capital for day-to-day business operations. Lease payments can be spread over several years. Payments are generally predictable and easier to budget for. There is an option to purchase the asset at the end of the lease term. Businesses can claim tax benefits on interest payments. Disadvantages of a finance lease: The lessee is often responsible for maintenance, insurance, and repairs. The business bears the risk of the asset becoming outdated or obsolete. Adds a liability to the balance sheet, which can impact debt ratios. The total cost over the lease term may sometimes be higher than buying the asset outright. Lease agreements are usually non-cancelable. So, there’s less flexibility. Missed lease payments can result in penalties and additional charges. Accounting and tax treatment of financial leases in India Under the Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 116, most financial leases are recorded on the lessee’s balance sheet. Instead of treating lease payments purely as an expense, the lessee recognizes a Right-of-Use (ROU) asset and a corresponding lease liability. Over the lease term, the right-of-use asset is depreciated, while the lease liability is reduced through periodic payments. The interest portion of the lease payment is generally recognized separately as a business cost and may be deductible subject to applicable tax rules. Since accounting and tax treatment can vary depending on the transaction and business structure, it is advisable to consult a qualified Chartered Accountant (CA) or tax professional before making any decisions. What are the examples of a finance lease? The finance lease meaning becomes easier to understand when we look at real-life business situations. A textile manufacturing company may lease a high-value cutter machine for the final production of garments. A transport company may lease a fleet of trucks to expand operations to different geographical locations. An IT firm may lease servers and data-storage equipment for its day-to-day operations. A construction company may lease heavy equipment, such as cranes, excavators, and earthmovers, for a long term. In each of these finance lease examples, the business gets access to equipment by agreeing to pay a few thousand rupees as lease payments. Acquiring these very assets may have cost them several lakhs. Who should opt for a finance lease? A finance lease is generally suitable for businesses that need to use expensive assets for a long period but do not want to pay a large upfront amount. It can be a good option for companies looking to preserve working capital while still gaining access to machinery, vehicles, equipment, or technology assets. However, businesses must be prepared to handle monthly lease payments, equipment maintenance and repair costs, and other ownership-related responsibilities during the lease term. Conclusion A financial lease allows businesses to get access to costly equipment, machinery, vehicles, and technology assets without making a large upfront investment. It allows companies to preserve their working capital for other financial needs. However, businesses must consider the risks involved before making a decision. A finance lease arrangement typically entails regular monthly payments, maintenance responsibilities, and the balance-sheet impact. A finance lease is a long-term arrangement that allows a business to use an asset without buying it immediately. The business makes regular lease payments over a fixed period while using the asset. Although the lessor remains the legal owner, the lessee takes on most of the responsibilities and benefits associated with the asset. What is the difference between a finance lease and an operating lease? A finance lease is usually long-term and transfers most ownership-related risks and rewards to the lessee. An operating lease is generally shorter and works more like a rental arrangement. In a finance lease, the lessee often has an option to buy the asset, while in an operating lease, the asset is typically returned to the lessor. Who owns the asset in a finance lease? In a finance lease, the legal ownership of the asset remains with the lessor throughout the lease period. However, the lessee gets the right to use the asset and usually takes responsibility for maintenance, insurance, and other ownership-related costs. In practice, the lessee bears many of the risks and rewards of ownership. Give an example of a finance lease. A common finance lease example is a manufacturing company leasing a machine worth several lakhs of rupees. Instead of paying the full amount upfront, the company makes periodic lease payments over several years while using the machine for production. At the end of the lease term, it may also get an option to purchase the machine. Is a finance lease shown on the balance sheet? Yes. Under the Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 116, a finance lease is generally reflected on the lessee's balance sheet. The lessee records a right-of-use asset and a corresponding lease liability. This gives a more complete picture of the company's financial obligations and asset usage. What are the tax benefits of a finance lease in India? The tax treatment of a finance lease depends on the specific transaction and applicable regulations. In general, depreciation on the leased asset and the interest component of lease payments are eligible for tax deductions under applicable rules. Since tax laws can change, businesses should consult a Chartered Accountant or tax advisor for guidance. Can the lessee buy the asset at the end of a finance lease? Yes, many finance leases include a purchase option at the end of the lease period. Depending on the agreement, the lessee may be able to buy the asset at a pre-agreed or bargained price, which is sometimes lower than the market value. However, the exact terms vary from one lease contract to another. strategy perfectly. The measure of this is gauged with key metrics such as IRR and MOIC. With one, you get the consistency and speed of your returns, while the other gives a total and absolute measure of return. metrics such as IRR and MOIC have helped investors and business owners to understand and measure VC funding success and returns – both as absolute and over time. Venture Capital (VC) is a crucial source of finance in today’s entrepreneurial world. The private market ecosystem thrives on VC funding and startup investing firms, as venture capital funds create value for investors and businesses. As value is created and returns are generated, the evaluation of VC funds is gauged with performance metrics such as Internal Rate of Return (IRR) and Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC). To understand how VC funds generate returns, we must first understand these performance metrics and why VC funds use them. Why do VC funds use IRR and MOIC? MOIC and IRR are popular measures used to evaluate investment performance in segments such as private equity, venture capital and real estate. These are investments that take years to mature, and these metrics help us measure the absolute wealth created and the speed and efficiency of such creation. For this reason, these two metrics are avidly used by fund managers to measure VC fund performance. IRR vs MOIC is an interesting combination, as both measure different aspects of VC fund performance. What is MOIC, and why is it important? As its name suggests, MOIC is expressed as a multiple. It gives us the absolute return on an investment, i.e., how much money has been generated out of the amount invested. Being a multiple like 2X and 3X, it is independent of time. It is measured as, MOIC = {Total Cash Distributions + Remaining Value} / Total Invested Capital or MOIC= Total Value/ Initial Investment For example, if the initial investment of a VC fund was Rs. 10 crores, and the exit value was Rs. 30 crores, the MOIC is 3X, i.e., the wealth generated was three times the invested capital. MOIC is a simple metric that highlights the total value created from an investment. What is IRR, and why is it important? Unlike MOIC, IRR is a rate and not a multiple. It considers the time taken to generate returns and gives the annualized rate of return on an investment. It measures how quickly an investment has compounded, and accounts for the time value of money. Two investments with the same MOIC can have very different IRRs. Consider the table below, Investment MOIC Holding Period Startup A 3X 3 years Startup B 3X 8 years Given the shorter time taken to generate an MOIC of 3X, Startup A will have a better IRR than Startup B. MOIC and IRR: Relative significance for investors and entrepreneurs MOIC and IRR are complementary metrics, and one cannot replace the other. For investors, MOIC provides a measure of, Straightforward metric that quantifies how many multiples of the initial investment were generated With IRR, investors gain an understanding of, The profitability of an investment, that takes into account time value of money. For a complete assessment of venture fund performance, professional investors evaluate IRR in conjunction with MOIC. Entrepreneurs seeking capital also benefit from understanding these metrics. It helps them understand the meaning of VC funding measures and engage in a meaningful conversation with investors. The merit of a VC investment lies in the profitability prospects of a startup. The startup has to deliver handsome returns within a reasonable time. To do so, it has to display scalability and the opportunity of a profitable exit. These can be measured conclusively using metrics like MOIC and IRR, and influence how VC funding works. The metrics reloaded As you gain understanding of the metrics, it is also important to understand the bigger picture, which is how a VC fund works. A VC fund pools money from investors, and the fund manager invests it with the expectation of high returns from the investments. The VC funding process involves Identifying promising startups for VC funding, Conducting due diligence, Getting the company VC funded in exchange for equity, Guiding business growth, Executing the exit strategy. The success of this entire operation is measured with the help of metrics, with IRR and MOIC being the prominent ones. Concluding thoughts Understanding metrics like MOIC and IRR helps us understand how investors assess their VC performance. In this regard, IRR and MOIC are particularly relevant in India’s expanding startup ecosystem. They will help investors and entrepreneurs understand how VC funds in India measure funding success and failure. Build Your Wealth with Expert Guidance from Tata Capital! It is the ecosystem where VC firms make equity investments in startups and promising high-growth businesses in India. How to approach VC for funding? Entrepreneurs and startup founders approach VC firms through networking events, accelerator programs, startup platforms or a direct approach, almost always with a strong pitch deck. How to start a VC fund? How to start a VC fund in India is something that can be considered with investment expertise, compliance, fundraising capacity and strategy. An investment management structure should be in place, which complies with the regulations applicable to private investment vehicles. What is a good IRR for venture capital investments? VC investors generally seek an annualized IRR of 30% at the early stage. This expectation may be lower in later-stage and growth equity investments, typically 20 - 25%. Do top VC funds in India disclose IRR and MOIC figures? Top VC funds in India are known to share IRR and MOIC information with their limited partners. However, detailed fund-level performance information may not be made public. invest. Designed with features of mutual funds and alternative investments, they offer greater flexibility and diverse themes and strategies. Their introduction reflects a rising demand for customized products beyond traditional investment funds. SEBI’s specialized investment funds mark an evolution in India’s investment ecosystem. It is an interesting hybrid of traditional mutual funds and alternative investment products. In the ever-evolving Indian investment landscape, mutual funds continue to be a dominant force in retail investing. Big-ticket investors can invest in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) , which provide access to a wider range of investment strategies and asset classes beyond traditional mutual funds. A specialized investment fund bridges the gap between mutual fund and alternative investment opportunities ( PMS & AIF ). Raising the bar on investment sophistication and minimum investment requirements, specialized investment funds offer access to advanced investment strategies that were previously available primarily through PMS and AIF structures. What is a specialized investment fund? The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) designed the specialized investment fund for fund managers to apply flexible and advanced strategies. The SIF investment fund fact-sheet: Minimum investment requirement of Rs. 10 lakhs across all SIF investments with an AMC. Advanced strategies like long-short equity and unhedged short positions using derivatives can be utilized, Funds are available in open-ended, close-ended, and interval strategies, Apart from equities and debts, specialized investment funds may invest across a broader opportunity set, including REITs , InvITs, derivatives, and other permitted securities, depending on the investment strategy. Registered Asset Management Companies (AMCs) meeting the SEBI Regulatory Framework can launch specialized investment funds. Why do specialized investment funds stand out? Specialized investment funds are aimed at pursuing more targeted investment themes and strategies, compared to traditional mutual funds. They stand out in the investment landscape with their, Greater portfolio flexibility, Access to niche investment themes, Flexible diversification opportunities, Wider choice of investment strategies Access to Derivatives in the portfolio Why are specialized investment funds gathering pace in India? Looking back at the evolution of the investment landscape in India, it is easier to understand the reasons why specialized investment funds are gaining attention. Traditional mutual funds evolved in the 1990s. They were aimed at tapping retail investors with mostly long-only strategies, and were guarded with stringent regulatory oversight. Lists of alternative investment funds and PMS came into prominence in the 2010s. These investments saw structures operate under separate regulatory frameworks and offer greater flexibility in portfolio construction and investment strategies.They have high entry barriers and aim to cater to high-net-worth individuals and institutions. SEBI introduced the specialized investment fund framework in 2025. With this, you get the pooled structure and transparency of mutual funds, with the strategic aggression of PMSs. This evolution means that investors can now achieve investment diversification beyond the traditional mutual fund strategies. How to combine specialized investment funds with existing portfolios? For retail investors, the emergence of specialized investment funds doesn’t warrant the replacement of existing investments. Instead, it can be used as a strategic addition and complement investments like, Traditional equity mutual funds, Debt mutual funds, Index funds, Alternative investment products. What is the future for specialized investment funds? Willing to capitalize their presence in this emerging category, AMCs are expected to intensify the launch of specialized investment funds. With this, the investment choices of retail investors are likely to mature as innovative offerings across themes and categories come into the spotlight. SEBI specialized investment funds are expected to provide Indian investors with a fresh new approach towards diversification, portfolio management and long-term wealth creation. A specialized investment fund provides greater flexibility in portfolio construction and investment strategies compared to traditional mutual funds, while remaining within a regulated framework. Why are SEBI specialized investment funds attracting attention? They offer investors a regulated avenue to access specialized strategies that may not be available through conventional mutual fund categories while maintaining oversight within the financial system. What are the alternative investment fund eligibility criteria in India? Eligibility requirements vary by fund category and investor type. Many alternative investment products are designed for sophisticated investors who can meet minimum investment thresholds prescribed by regulations. Who can invest in a Specialized Investment Fund (SIF)? Investors who meet the minimum investment threshold of ₹10 lakh with a particular AMC can invest in SIFs, subject to the terms of the scheme. Should I replace my mutual funds with Specialized Investment Funds (SIFs)? No. SIFs are generally designed to complement, not replace, traditional mutual funds. Investors may use SIFs for a portion of their portfolio to access specialized strategies, while continuing to rely on mutual funds for core portfolio exposure and diversification. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Summary Stablecoins are digital currencies that are attached to reserve assets like national currency, gold, government securities, etc. Being blockchain-based, stablecoins maintain the digital currency benefits while minimizing the notorious crypto volatility. Stablecoins can be currency-backed, commodity-backed, crypto-backed, or in algorithmic forms. India is planning to launch its stablecoin, ARC, which will ride on the Reserve Bank of India’s ( RBI’s) Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) ecosystem. Stablecoins are digital currencies that are linked to a reserve asset, thus reducing price volatility while retaining blockchain efficiency. Popular cryptocurrency, Bitcoin, has an annualized volatility of more than 40%. Fluctuating purely on the balance of supply and demand, this decentralized currency is known for its volatility. Cryptocurrency can shed this volatility if a reserve asset is attached to it. Stablecoins do exactly that by maintaining a link to a reserve asset. Such a reserve asset can be fiat currencies, commodities or financial instruments. What is Stablecoin? Stablecoin is a highly practical innovation in the digital asset ecosystem. Its link to a reserve asset ensures that it maintains a relatively stable value. Stablecoin meaning is ingrained in two key words: “price stability”. Stablecoin price may be pegged to underlying assets such as US Dollar Euro Gold Government securities Other cryptocurrencies, etc. Also, read – Fundamentals of pension withdrawal What is a stablecoin development company? A stablecoin development company develops digital currencies that can be pegged to a reserve asset. They ensure that the stablecoin is customized, secure and updated with the regulations. A stablecoin development company manages the end-to-end infrastructure of the stablecoin, which includes Smart contract creation Liquidity planning Reserve management, and Multi-chain deployment Also, read – What is a ULIP Plan? Why was a stablecoin developed? Traditional cryptocurrencies have been struggling to maintain stability and have experienced extreme short-term volatility. Stablecoins were introduced primarily to address this challenge. Stablecoins reduce exposure to market fluctuations. It allows blockchain-based transactions. It supports Decentralized Finance (DeFi) applications. It enables faster cross-border remittances. It adds liquidity to the crypto market. What are the different types of stablecoins? The table below explains the different types of stablecoins, with examples. Type Feature Example Fiat-collateralized stablecoins They maintain reserves of fiat currencies USDT (Tether), FDUSD (First Digital USD) Commodity-backed stablecoins They track the value of physical assets PAG (PAX Gold), KAG (Kinesis Silver) Crypto-collateralized stablecoins They track the value of cryptocurrencies DAI (Ethereum blockchain-based stablecoin) Algorithmic stablecoins Price stability is maintained through algorithms and supply adjustments FRAX (backed fractionally by algorithm and collaterals) Also, read – Saving Schemes for the girl child in India Which are the most popular stablecoins in the world? A list of stablecoins that are among the most popular in the world as of now is provided below: Stablecoin Pegged Asset Category Primary Use USDT (Tether) US Dollar Fiat-backed Trading and payments USDC US Dollar Fiat-backed Institutional and retail transactions DAI US Dollar Crypto-backed Decentralized finance FDUSD US Dollar Fiat-backed Exchange settlements PAX Gold (PAXG) Gold Commodity-backed Gold exposure through blockchain The table also indicates the specific transactional or investment usage of stablecoins. Also, read – What is CAGR in mutual funds? Where does India stand in stablecoin use and development? The RBI- was quick to announce the launch of its digital currency, CBDC-. However, it has maintained a cautious approach towards stablecoins. However, the Asset Reserve Certificate (ARC) is tipped to be India’s very own stablecoin. Here are a few basic details on ARC: ARC will track the value of the Indian National Rupee. It will be collateralized 1:1 against cash and cash equivalents such as government securities and treasury bills. WazirX, Polygon and fintech firm Anq are involved in the design and development of the ARC. ARC will have a two-tier framework. The CBDC will handle final settlements, while ARC will provide a layer for programmable payments, smart contracts, and decentralized finance. ARC will be expected to curb the outflow of domestic liquidity to USD-backed stablecoins. ARC will initially be rolled out to meet the needs of corporate and institutional accounts. Like elsewhere, a stablecoin in India is expected to be used for international remittances and business payments, merchant settlements, treasury management, digital asset trading, etc. Also, read – Types of mutual funds in India Final word Stablecoins are a significant development in the blockchain-based financial ecosystem. Stablecoins provide the efficiency of digital assets with the stability of traditional currencies. In India, blockchain adoption is at a nascent stage, and regulatory clarity is a work in progress. Nevertheless, it is an area that Indian investors and businesses need to keep a close watch on. Build Your Wealth with Expert Guidance from Tata Capital! Yes. You can buy stablecoins through cryptocurrency exchanges that support the Indian rupee. You will need to ensure KYC verification, account funding through banking channels, and then place the order for the desired stablecoin. How does a stablecoin comply with regulations? The issuer that creates a stablecoin generally needs to fulfill legal frameworks and ensure that reserve management systems, smart contract infrastructure, audit mechanisms, and compliance processes, such as Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Know-Your-Customer (KYC) requirements, are in place. How many stablecoins are in circulation in the global cryptocurrency ecosystem? While there are more than 200 stablecoins in circulation across the world, a small minority forms the majority of the market value and trading volume. The exact number keeps changing as new stablecoins are launched, while some become inactive. Why are businesses using stablecoins? Stablecoins are helping businesses to streamline cross-border payments, reduce currency conversion costs, improve treasury management, and settle transactions with more speed and accuracy. Can I invest in stablecoins and earn returns? Yes, you can earn returns from stablecoins. You can lend stablecoins, participate in liquidity pools, or use staking and yield-generating protocols. The returns may bear inherent risk and would vary with market conditions and platform policies. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund When it comes to funding your business, both business loans and SME loans can get you the capital you need. But they are not the same thing. They differ in scale, eligibility criteria, and what you can use the money for. Picking the wrong one can mean higher costs, stricter terms, or even rejection. Picking the right one can make a real difference to your growth. This guide explains what each option means, how they compare side by side, who qualifies, what interest rates to expect, and how to decide which SME business loan is the better fit for you. What is a Business Loan? A business loan is financing that a business borrows to cover a wide range of needs, from expanding operations and buying equipment to managing working capital or hiring staff. These loans are offered to established businesses and can be either secured (backed by collateral) or unsecured. Loan amounts generally range from a few lakhs to several crores based on the lender and your business profile. End uses include inventory purchase, office expansion, product launches, and more. Lenders like Tata Capital offer structured business loans with flexible repayment terms suited to different business stages and requirements. What is an SME Loan? So, what is an SME loan? It is financing specifically designed for Small and Medium Enterprises that fall under India’s MSME or Udyam registration classification. Unlike standard business loans, an SME loan is built around the realities of smaller businesses. For example, shorter operating histories, leaner documentation, and tighter cash flows. These loans typically come with relaxed eligibility criteria and are often backed by government schemes like CGTMSE, making them more accessible. An SME business loan can fund equipment purchases, working capital needs, inventory, or even marketing efforts, giving smaller enterprises the financial push they need to grow steadily. Types of SME Loans There are several SME loan options available, depending on what your business needs: Term Loan : A lump sum borrowed for a fixed period, ideal for planned investments like infrastructure or expansion. SME Working Capital Loan: Covers day-to-day operational expenses like salaries, inventory, and vendor payments. Equipment Finance : Specifically for purchasing or upgrading machinery and business equipment. Government-Backed Schemes: Programmes like CGTMSE and Mudra offer SME business loans with lower collateral requirements and subsidised interest rates for eligible enterprises. Learn More – Working Capital Loan Business Loan vs SME Loan: Key Differences (Comparison Table) Both business loans and SME loans fund business growth. But the terms, eligibility, and scale differ significantly. Here’s a side-by-side breakdown: Feature SME Loan Business Loan Eligibility MSMEs registered under Udyam/MSME classification Established businesses with strong financials Loan Amount Typically ₹1 lakh – ₹2 crore ₹2 crore and above Interest Rate Lower; often subsidised by government schemes Market-driven; varies by lender and profile Collateral Often not required May be required for larger amounts Documentation Minimal – GST, KYC, basic financials Extensive – audited statements, credit history Repayment Tenure Up to 60 months Up to 48-84 months, depending on the lender End Use Working capital, equipment, day-to-day ops Expansion, new branches, large asset purchase Best Suited For Small and growing enterprises Mid-to-large businesses scaling rapidly Eligibility: Business Loan vs SME Loan Eligibility is one of the biggest practical differences between the two. Here’s what lenders typically look for: For a Business Loan: Business vintage of 3+ years with stable revenues Minimum annual turnover of ₹1 crore or more Strong CIBIL score (typically 700+) Audited financials, ITR, and property documents may be required For an SME Business Loan: Business vintage of 2-3 years Turnover as low as ₹4 lakhs in some cases Udyam/MSME registration strengthens eligibility Relaxed credit score requirements; basic KYC, GST, and bank statements are usually sufficient Interest Rates: Business Loan vs SME Loan Business loan interest rates vary based on your CIBIL score , loan amount, tenure, and whether the loan is secured or unsecured. SME loans often benefit from government scheme subsidies , bringing rates down further for eligible borrowers. Loan Type Typical Interest Rate Key Factors Business Loan 12% – 24% p.a. Credit score, collateral, tenure, lender SME Loan 8% – 18% p.a. Udyam status, scheme subsidy, turnover Lenders like Tata Capital offer competitive rates on both products. Before applying, use an EMI calculator to map repayments against your cash flow. Which Loan Should You Choose? The right call depends on where your business stands today. Choose a Business Loan if: Your business is well-established with 3+ years of operation. You need a larger loan amount for expansion, acquisition, or infrastructure. You have a strong CIBIL score and can provide documentation. Speed of disbursal matters more than rate. Choose an SME Business Loan if: You run a small or growing enterprise registered under Udyam/MSME. You want lower rates, minimal paperwork, or government-scheme benefits. Your credit profile is still building. You need working capital quickly without collateral. Still unsure? Tata Capital’s loan advisors can help you evaluate both business loans and SME options based on your actual profile. How to Get a Business Loan? Here’s the step-by-step process on how to get a business loan in India: Step 1: Check Your Eligibility Review the lender’s criteria for business vintage, turnover, and credit score before applying. Step 2: Check Eligibility Confirm you meet the lender’s turnover, vintage, and documentation requirements. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund When your business needs short-term funds to keep things moving, two options come up most often: cash credit vs overdraft. Both let you borrow up to a set limit and pay interest only on what you actually use, not the entire sanctioned amount. That makes them far more flexible than a term loan . But they are not the same thing. They differ in how they work, what collateral is needed, who qualifies, and what they are best suited for. In this overdraft vs cash credit guide, we cover clear definitions of both, a side-by-side comparison, eligibility, and a simple framework to help you choose the right facility for your business. What is Cash Credit? Cash credit (CC) is a secured, short-term working capital facility offered primarily to businesses. It allows you to borrow money against collateral through a process called hypothecation. The bank sets a credit limit based on your “drawing power,” which is calculated as a percentage of the value of your pledged assets. You don’t need to withdraw the full amount at once. You draw only what you need, when you need it, and interest is charged only on the amount utilised. In cash credit vs overdraft comparisons, CC is the go-to option for funding day-to-day business operations. Read More – Different Types of Loans Available in India What is an Overdraft? An overdraft (OD) is a facility that lets you withdraw more money than what is currently available in your bank account, up to a pre-approved limit. It is linked to your current or savings account. This means when your balance hits zero, you can still make payments, issue cheques, or transfer funds without any disruption. An overdraft can be secured or unsecured, depending on your relationship with the bank and credit profile. In the overdraft vs cash credit debate, OD is more flexible in collateral terms. Interest in cash credit and overdraft facilities is charged only on the amount actually overdrawn, not the full limit. Read More – Overdrafts on Home Loans Cash Credit vs Overdraft: Key Differences (Comparison Table) Both facilities let you borrow as needed and pay interest only on what you use. But the cash credit and overdraft difference becomes clear when you look at the details: Feature Cash Credit (CC) Overdraft (OD) Definition Borrowing against pledged business assets up to a drawing power limit Withdrawing beyond the account balance up to a sanctioned limit Collateral Required – typically inventory, stock, or receivables May or may not be required; can be FD, property, or unsecured Eligibility Primarily businesses Both individuals and businesses Interest Calculation Charged on the daily utilised balance Charged on the amount overdrawn from the account Tenure/Renewal Typically 12 months; renewed annually with stock statements Short-term; reviewed quarterly, renewed annually Best Suited For Businesses needing regular working capital Individuals or businesses managing short-term cash flow gaps In the cash credit vs overdraft decision, the core question is simple: are you a business needing structured working capital, or do you need a flexible buffer for occasional shortfalls? Difference in Collateral and Security Collateral is where the cash credit and overdraft difference is most significant in practice. Cash credit is almost always secured. The bank requires you to pledge business assets like stock, inventory, or receivables. Your borrowing limit is directly tied to their value. An overdraft is more flexible. It can be secured against a fixed deposit, property, or securities. In some cases, it may also be offered unsecured based on your credit profile and banking relationship. For businesses without significant liquid assets, an OD can be easier to access in cash credit vs overdraft situations. Difference in Eligibility and Purpose In the overdraft vs cash credit comparison, eligibility and purpose draw a clear line. Cash credit is designed exclusively for manufacturers, traders, or retailers who need ongoing funds to manage inventory, raw materials, or receivables. Overdraft, on the other hand, is available to both individuals and businesses. It suits anyone needing a short-term liquidity buffer. Cash credit and overdraft serve different users with different financial rhythms. Read More – Types of Working Capital Difference in Interest and Limit In both facilities, interest is charged only on the amount you actually use, not the full sanctioned limit. That said, the two work differently. In cash credit vs overdraft, the CC limit fluctuates based on your drawing power, which is the value of your pledged stock or receivables at any given time. Your limit can change as inventory levels change. An OD limit is fixed upfront by the bank based on your account history, income, or collateral. The cash credit and overdraft difference in rates is marginal, and both vary by lender and borrower profile. Similarities Between Cash Credit and Overdraft It’s easy to confuse the two because cash credit and overdraft share several features: Both are revolving, short-term credit facilities, meaning you borrow, repay, and borrow again within the limit. Both charge interest only on the amount utilised, not the full sanctioned limit. Both come with a defined credit limit set by the lender. Both require periodic review and annual renewal. These similarities are exactly why the cash credit vs overdraft question comes up so often. Read More – What Is SME Smart Score Which is Better for Your Business: Cash Credit or Overdraft? The right choice depends on how your business uses funds day to day. Choose Cash Credit if: You regularly need working capital to manage stock, inventory, or raw materials. You have business assets to pledge as collateral. You want a structured facility with a higher limit tied to your business volume. Choose Overdraft if: You need occasional, flexible access to funds for short-term cash flow gaps. You prefer a facility linked directly to your existing bank account. You want secured or unsecured options without pledging business inventory. Still weighing the cash credit vs overdraft decision? Tata Capital offers tailored business finance solutions to help you pick the right working capital facility for your specific needs. What is the difference between cash credit and overdraft? Both cash credit and overdraft are practical working capital tools. The right one depends on your collateral availability, business purpose, and cash flow pattern. If you need structured, inventory-backed funding regularly, cash credit works better. If you need flexible, account-linked access for occasional gaps, an overdraft fits more naturally. For larger funding needs, a business loan may be worth exploring, too. In the cash credit vs overdraft decision, Tata Capital can help you find the right fit. Individuals looking for a similar short-term credit buffer are better suited to an overdraft facility instead. How is interest charged on cash credit and overdraft? In both facilities, the cash credit and overdraft difference in interest calculation is minimal. You pay interest only on the amount actually utilised, not the full sanctioned limit. For regular working capital needs, cash credit is generally the better fit in the cash credit vs overdraft decision. It offers higher limits tied to your business assets and is structured for ongoing operational use. lead to loan rejections . For example, a wrong account status, an incorrect outstanding balance, a loan you never took, etc. The good news is that raising a CIBIL dispute is simple, free, and does not affect your credit score in any way. This guide covers everything you need to know: what a CIBIL dispute is, the types of errors that commonly appear, how to raise a dispute in CIBIL online, and what the resolution process looks like. What is a CIBIL Dispute? Banks and NBFCs report your credit data to CIBIL every month. And while this process is mostly accurate, errors can still happen. A typo during data upload, a delayed loan closure update, or even identity theft can result in wrong information appearing on your report. A CIBIL dispute is a formal request you submit to TransUnion CIBIL asking them to correct inaccurate, incomplete, or outdated information in your credit report. Raising a dispute in CIBIL is completely free and does not impact your credit score in any way. Read More – CIBIL score vs. credit score Common Errors You Can Dispute in Your CIBIL Report If you spot any of the following, it’s worth raising a CIBIL dispute right away: Wrong personal details: Spelling errors in your name, PAN, date of birth, or address. Incorrect account information: Wrong loan amount, incorrect EMI, or payment status marked overdue despite timely payments. Accounts that aren’t yours: Raise a dispute in CIBIL for loans or credit cards you never took out, which could indicate identity theft or fraud. Duplicate accounts: The same loan or credit card appearing twice, making your debt look higher than it is. Closed loans still showing active: Fully repaid loans or settled credit cards still reflecting as outstanding. Read More – How Much CIBIL Score Required For Personal Loan How to Raise a Dispute in CIBIL Online (Step-by-Step)? Here is exactly how to raise a dispute in CIBIL online: Step 1: Log in to Your myCIBIL Account Visit cibil.com and sign in with your credentials. If you don’t have an account, register first and access your latest credit report. Step 2: Go to Credit Reports > Dispute Centre Inside your dashboard, navigate to the Credit Reports section and click on Dispute Centre. Step 3: Click ‘Dispute an Item’ This opens the official CIBIL raise a dispute form, where you can flag errors. Step 4: Select the Section with the Error Choose the relevant section from personal information, account details, and payment history, wherever the mistake appears. Step 5: Choose the Dispute Type and Enter Correct Details Specify what is wrong and provide the accurate information. You can raise a dispute in CIBIL for multiple errors within a single submission. Step 6: Submit and Save Your Confirmation Once submitted, the disputed fields are tagged “Under Dispute.” You will receive a confirmation with a dispute ID to track progress. Read More – How long does it take to improve your CIBIL score? CIBIL Dispute Login: Accessing the Dispute Centre To complete the CIBIL dispute login, follow these steps: Visit cibil.com and click ‘Login’ on the homepage. Enter your registered email or mobile number and password. Or log in via OTP. Once inside your myCIBIL dashboard, navigate to Credit Reports > Dispute Centre. No account yet? Click ‘Get Your CIBIL Score’ to register first. It only takes a few minutes. Then, you can file your CIBIL dispute. How to Check Your CIBIL Dispute Status? Once you have submitted your dispute, tracking it is simple. Here’s how to check your CIBIL dispute status: Log in to your myCIBIL account using your CIBIL dispute login credentials. Navigate to the Dispute Centre. You will see all previously raised disputes listed here. Check the status against your dispute ID. It will typically show as Under Dispute, In Progress, Resolved, or Rejected. If resolved, your credit report will be updated automatically, and your score recalculated. CIBIL also sends email and SMS updates at key stages, so you don’t need to log in repeatedly to stay informed. Also Read – What are the 4 CICs in India? CIBIL Dispute Resolution Process and Timeline Once you submit your dispute, the CIBIL dispute resolution process follows a clear path. As per RBI norms, the standard turnaround is 30 days. Here’s what happens step by step: Day 0: Submission Your disputed fields are immediately tagged “Under Dispute” in your credit report within 24-48 hours. Days 1-25: Lender verification CIBIL contacts the relevant bank or NBFC that submitted the data and asks them to confirm or deny the error. Days 25-30: Resolution If the lender confirms the mistake, CIBIL corrects your report and removes the “Under Dispute” tag. Post-resolution: Score update Your credit score is recalculated within 5-7 days of the correction. If the CIBIL dispute is not resolved within 30 days, CIBIL is liable to pay compensation under its framework. What If Your CIBIL Dispute Is Rejected? A rejected CIBIL dispute is not a dead end. Here’s how you can escalate it: Re-raise with stronger documents: Attach your loan closure letter, NOC, and payment proof together to make a stronger case for CIBIL dispute resolution. Contact the lender directly: Email the bank or NBFC’s grievance redressal officer with your dispute reference number. They are required to respond within 30 days. Write to CIBIL’s grievance officer: Formally request a review through CIBIL’s internal grievance mechanism. Escalate to the RBI Ombudsman: If both CIBIL and the lender fail to resolve it, file a complaint under the RBI’s Credit Information Companies Ombudsman scheme. Read More – How to build a credit score from scratch Does Raising a CIBIL Dispute Affect Your Credit Score? This is one of the most common concerns. And the answer is no. Raising a CIBIL dispute does not negatively affect your credit score in any way. When you flag an error, the disputed field is simply marked “Under Dispute” while the verification is underway. Your score remains untouched during this period. In fact, if the error was pulling your score down, a successful correction can actually improve it. So there is no reason to hesitate. Raise a dispute in CIBIL as soon as you spot a mistake. Tips to Avoid CIBIL Errors in the Future A little vigilance goes a long way in avoiding a CIBIL dispute altogether: Check your credit report at least once a year, as early detection can ensure quick CIBIL dispute resolution. Collect your NOC after every loan closure and verify within 60-90 days that the account status has been updated correctly. Keep your contact details current with lenders, as outdated information is a common source of data mismatches. Watch for unknown accounts that may indicate fraud. Conclusion CIBIL errors are more common than most people realise. But cbut they are fixable. A timely CIBIL dispute can protect your credit score, restore your loan eligibility, and prevent unnecessary rejections down the line. The process is free, fully online, and does not hurt your score. So if something looks wrong on your report, do not wait. Review it, raise the dispute, and get it corrected. Once your report is accurate, check your eligibility for a Tata Capital loan with confidence.
