Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Summary A loan repayment schedule is a detailed timetable indicating how and when you must repay the borrowed money. It lists the due dates and payment amounts, and breaks down the principal and interest for each payment. It also mentions the remaining loan amount after you make your payment. After referring to the payment schedule, you can plan your monthly budget and see how much total interest you will pay over time. The schedule also helps you stay on track to avoid late fees. A loan repayment schedule provides a structured plan outlining how you will repay the borrowedamount over a specific period. When a lender approves a loan, it provides a loan repayment schedule, listing every Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) you need to pay over the loan tenure. The schedule shows both the principal and interest component. This guide explains what a loan repayment schedule is, what it includes, how it is calculated, and how you can use it to manage your loan effectively. What is a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule, or a payment schedule, meaning the document lenders provide when your loan is approved is a table with all the necessary loan repayment details. It clearly shows every EMI from start to finish, the interest charged, how much you still owe, and when your loan will be fully repaid. It makes financial planning much easier and saves you from surprises later. What does a loan repayment schedule contain? The components of a loan repayment schedule are as follows: Component Meaning EMI number The sequence of each monthly payment. EMI due date The date on which you need to pay EMI. EMI amount The total amount you pay every month. Principal component The portion of the EMI that reduces your loan amount. Interest component The portion of the EMI charged as interest by the lender. Outstanding principal balance The remaining loan amount after each EMI is paid. In a standard reducing-balance loan, the interest component is higher in the initial EMIs because it is calculated on a larger outstanding principal. As you repay the loan, the principal balance decreases, so the interest portion reduces while the principal component gradually increases. How is a loan repayment schedule calculated? To calculate the loan repayment schedule, most lenders use the reducing-balance (amortization) method. Here, monthly interest is calculated on the outstanding principal, and the remaining portion of the EMI is applied to reduce the principal. Since the outstanding balance decreases with each payment, the interest charged on the next EMI is lower. To calculate EMI, you can use the formula given below: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1) Where, P = principal loan amount r = monthly interest rate n = loan tenure (in months) Here’s an illustrative example for better understanding. Suppose you borrow Rs. 5 lakh for 5 years at an interest rate of 10% per annum. You will have a fixed EMI of Rs. 10,624, and a total interest payout of Rs. 1,37,411. The first few EMIs will contain more interest than principal. Gradually, the interest portion will decrease while the principal repayment will increase. You can use an online EMI calculator to instantly generate a detailed payment schedule. Also Read – Loan vs. Advance What is the importance of a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule is important for several reasons, such as: Planning your budget: You can track EMI amounts and due dates. Knowing your interest cost: It shows the total interest payable over the loan tenure. Deciding on prepayments: You can estimate potential interest savings. Planning taxes: It helps you keep track of eligible tax benefits on the loan. Comparing loans: You can evaluate different loan offers based on the total repayment cost. How to get your loan repayment schedule? Your lender usually provides a loan repayment schedule when the loan is disbursed. You can also download it at any time through your online loan account or customer portal. If you are planning a new loan, use Tata Capital’s EMI Calculator to estimate your repayment schedule and manage your loan with confidence. What are the tips to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively? If you want to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively, here are some helpful tips: Set up auto-debit: Enable NACH or auto-debit to avoid missing EMI payments. Check before prepaying: Review your schedule to estimate possible interest savings. Request an updated schedule: Ask your lender for a revised schedule if your floating interest rate changes. Track principal repayments: Keep a record of the principal repaid each year for home loan tax filing purposes. Also Read – What is Part-Payment, Pre-Payment, Pre-Closure of Loan? Conclusion A loan repayment schedule is an important financial planning tool that shows how each EMI is divided between principal and interest. It helps you manage your cash flow and make informed prepayment decisions. The actual repayment schedule depends on your loan amount, interest rate, and tenure, and thus, do not refer to the standard ones available online. High Mark. Lenders evaluate the credit reports from one or more of these bureaus before approving your loan. The Equifax credit score, Experian, and CIBIL score usually range from 300 to 900. However, they differ based on levels of trust, update speeds, and data rules. TransUnion CIBIL is the oldest and most trusted credit bureau, Experian is a major global bureau, while Equifax is known for data analytics. Experian, CIBIL, CRIF High Mark, and Equifax credit scores are important factors lenders consider for loan approval. These scores are generated by collecting financial data. India has four RBI-licensed credit bureaus: Experian, CIBIL (TransUnion), Equifax, and CRIF High Mark. Each bureau generates its own credit score , which often confuses borrowers. This guide explains the Experian Credit score , Equifax credit score, why scores differ across bureaus, and which one matters most to lenders. Which are India’s four credit bureaus? An overview CIBIL, Experian, Equifax, and High Mark (CRIF) collect credit data from lenders to generate credit reports and scores under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. Credit bureau Brief introduction TransUnion CIBIL India’s oldest and most widely used credit bureau. Experian India A global credit bureau offering credit reports and scores. Equifax India It provides credit information and credit scores. CRIF High Mark It offers credit reports for individuals and businesses. What is the CIBIL score? CIBIL (TransUnion CIBIL) is the oldest credit bureau in India and most widely used by lenders. Its CIBIL score ranges from 300 to 900 , wherein a score of 750 or above is generally considered good. Since most lenders check this score, “CIBIL score” is often used as a general term for credit scores in India. What is the Experian credit score? Experian India also provides a credit score ranging from 300 to 900. Like the TransUnion CIBIL score, the Experian CIBIL score is based on your credit history. However, Experian may use a different scoring model and receive data from some lenders that CIBIL does not, and vice versa. What is the Equifax credit score? The Equifax credit score is provided by Equifax India and ranges from 1 to 999. This range is the primary difference between Equifax and Experian. Some banks and NBFCs use the Equifax credit score as an alternative or additional check when assessing loan applications. Also Read – CIBIL score vs. credit score CIBIL vs Experian vs Equifax: What are the key differences? The following table highlights the differences between CIBIL and Experian and the differences between Equifax and Experian. Feature TransUnion CIBIL Experian India Equifax India CRIF High Mark Parent company TransUnion Experian plc Equifax Inc. CRIF S.p.A. Score range 300-900 300-900 1-999 300-900 Data sources Varies by lender reporting Varies by lender reporting Varies by lender reporting Varies by lender reporting Lender preference Most widely used by banks and NBFCs Used by some lenders Used by some lenders Used by some lenders Why are your CIBIL and Experian scores different? If you are wondering why Experian and CIBIL scores are different for you, here are the simple reasons: Different lender reporting: Not all lenders report to every bureau. Different scoring models: Each bureau uses its own scoring method. Update timing: Credit information may be updated on different dates. Dispute status: A corrected error may appear in one bureau before another. Also Read – Credit Rating vs. Credit Score Which credit score do lenders check? Most banks and NBFCs in India commonly check the CIBIL score when evaluating a loan application. However, some lenders use Experian, Equifax, or CRIF High Mark as their primary bureau or as an additional check. To improve your loan approval chances, you must maintain a healthy credit score across all four credit bureaus , not just CIBIL. How to check your credit score across all bureaus? You can check your credit score on the official websites of the different bureaus. Each bureau offers one free credit report every year, as per the RBI mandate. Check all four reports periodically to spot errors or score differences and raise disputes if needed. What are the tips to improve your credit score across all bureaus? If you want to improve your credit score across all bureaus, here are some tips to follow: Pay bills and dues on time: Never miss EMI or credit card payments. Keep usage low: Use less than 30% of your credit limit. Limit applications: Avoid multiple loan inquiries within a short time. Check reports: Review all bureau reports and dispute errors promptly. Maintain balance: Keep a healthy mix of secured and unsecured credit. Eligible borrowers can opt for Tata Capital Personal Loans and Business Loans to meet funding needs responsibly. Conclusion CIBIL is India’s most widely used credit bureau. However, the others, such as Experian, Equifax, and CRIF High Mark, also matter. The scores of different bureaus vary because of data coverage and scoring methods. You must try to maintain a healthy score across all bureaus. without pledging property or other security. Loans up to ₹7.5 lakh may qualify under government-backed schemes, while higher amounts depend on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant profile. For abroad studies, unsecured options may also be available through some lenders for eligible students. A student who wants to study abroad may be able to obtain an education loan without collateral, depending on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant’s financial profile. There is no need to pledge property, a fixed deposit, or another asset to obtain an education loan. In India, government-backed credit guarantee schemes can cover eligible education loans up to ₹7.5 lakh without collateral or a third-party guarantee. Higher collateral-free financing may also be available depending on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant’s financial profile. What is a Collateral-Free Education Loan? A study loan without collateral is for higher education and does not require you to pledge property, a fixed deposit, or any other asset as security. The lender will assess other factors such as the student’s course, institution, and co-applicant’s income and credit history. Government-backed credit guarantee assistance is also available for eligible loans up to ₹7.5 lakh under CGFSEL. The ₹7.5 Lakh Rule: Where Collateral-Free Is Guaranteed With the IBA Model Education Loan Scheme, education loans may be approved without the need for collateral or a third-party guarantee. The Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Education Loans (CGFSEL), managed by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC), offers a government-backed credit guarantee covering eligible assistance up to ₹7.5 lakh. The scheme guarantees payment against default to the lending institution, so it reduces the lender’s credit risk but does not mean that every applicant is automatically approved for a loan. Note that the ₹7.5 lakh represents the collateral-free limit within the CGFSEL framework. In the case of loans that are covered by the scheme, the borrower is not required to offer property, a fixed deposit, or some other asset as security. The scheme may be relevant when applying through banks under the IBA framework. Here is how the ₹7.5 lakh limit of the non-collateral education loan works: Loan amount Collateral/guarantee requirement Margin under the IBA Model Scheme Up to ₹4 lakh No collateral security or third-party guarantee Nil Above ₹4 lakh up to ₹7.5 lakh No collateral security or third-party guarantee under CGFSEL Around 5% for studies in India and around 15% for studies abroad Note: The CGFSEL guarantee is subject to the scheme’s eligibility conditions and applies through participating lending institutions. If a borrower has a grievance regarding CGFSEL, NCGTC provides a grievance mechanism where the borrower can select the scheme and bank and submit complaint details. NCGTC also provides a dedicated email address and contact number for CGFEL grievances and queries. Collateral-Free Education Loans for Studying Abroad It can be harder to obtain a collateral free education loan for abroad because overseas education can cost ₹25 lakh to ₹80 lakh or more. The CGFSEL framework covers eligible assistance up to ₹7.5 lakh, so larger funding requirements generally depend on lender-specific unsecured products. So, to secure larger funding amounts over 7.5 lakhs, you may have three options. Premier-institution unsecured loans Some banks offer higher-value student loans without collateral to students enrolled in premier institutions or universities. Depending on the lender, institution, course, and the applicant’s and co-applicant’s eligibility, collateral-free loan amounts may range from ₹50 lakh to up to ₹1 crore. Higher overall loan limits may be available, but these may require collateral. NBFC/fintech education loans Specialised education loan providers such as Credila, Avanse and Propelld provide unsecured funding to eligible students. While these no collateral education loans can be more flexible and may be processed more quickly, they may be available at higher interest costs than secured education loans. Tata Capital also provides collateral-free education loans for eligible domestic and overseas education requirements, with options up to ₹85 lakh, subject to eligibility criteria. PM-Vidyalaxmi PM-Vidyalaxmi scheme offers education loans without requiring any collateral or a guarantor to students admitted on merit to eligible Quality Higher Education Institutions (QHEIs) in India. The scheme covers 902 QHEIs. It does not provide funding for a foreign university simply because the student is studying abroad. Lenders may assess the university’s rank and reputation, the employability of the course, the country, the applicant’s academic record, the co-applicant’s income, credit history, and repayment ability before approving your loan application. A lower-ranked university with weak employment prospects may not be eligible for unsecured financing even if the student has an admission offer. So, before applying for the collateral free education loan, you should look at the approved-institution list, maximum unsecured limit, interest rate, and co-applicant requirements rather than assuming that every overseas admission qualifies. Government Schemes That Help (CGFSEL, PM-Vidyalaxmi, CSIS) Before applying for a commercial education loan without security, check whether you are eligible for a government-backed programme because such schemes may eliminate the need for security or reduce the interest rate. The rules and the income limits may change, so it is important to verify the most up-to-date requirements before applying for a non-collateral education loan. The students whose annual family income is up to ₹8 lakh may receive a 3% interest subsidy during the moratorium period on the eligible education-loan amount of up to ₹10 lakh. For information on education loans and the schemes, you can use the Vidya Lakshmi portal and the official PM-Vidyalaxmi information provided by the Ministry of Education. Eligibility and Documents Obtaining a non-collateral education loan involves more than submitting the admission letter. Because no property or other asset is pledged, lenders check the academic record, course, university, and the financial strength of your co-applicant. Key eligibility factors Key requirements to become eligible for a loan include: Confirmed Admission: You should have the admission letter from an eligible or approved institution. Course: Lenders prefer courses that have good career and employment prospects. STEM and other career-focused programmes may get closer consideration. Co-applicant income and credit score: Lenders may assess important factors such as the co-applicant’s income, CIBIL score , employment stability, and existing financial obligations to approve your collateral-free education loan for abroad. Academic record: Marks obtained in Class 10, 12, and at graduation can strengthen your education loan application. Tata Capital’s eligibility criteria include a minimum academic qualification of 60%, subject to the applicable product terms. Visa and admission proof: Admission letter and visa documents are necessary while applying for an education loan. Documents Required The essential documents for a education loan collateral free are: Admission letter Academic marksheets and certificates ID and address proof Co-applicant’s income documents and other KYC documents Course fee structure Interest Rates, Moratorium and the Real Cost An unsecured education loan for abroad may have a higher interest rate than a secured loan because no property or other asset is pledged. Tata Capital currently offers education loan rates ranging from 9.50% to 21%. The exact rate is determined according to the borrower and the loan terms. Interest generally continues to accrue during the moratorium period. If the borrower does not service the interest during this period, the unpaid interest may be capitalised and increase the outstanding loan balance, subject to the applicable loan terms and scheme conditions. For example, on a loan of ₹20 lakh at a rate of 10.5%, the interest amounts to approximately ₹2.1 lakh over one year. If unpaid interest is capitalised, this can increase the outstanding balance and the eventual repayment cost. So, if possible, the interest should be paid during the moratorium period to keep the final loan cost lower. When applying for a collateral-free education loan abroad, you should compare the interest rate, processing fees, moratorium terms, repayment period, and the total amount to be repaid. You should also look at the lender’s Key Facts Statement (KFS), because it provides important information regarding the loan’s annualised cost and charges. Tax Benefit: Section 80E A study loan without collateral can also provide a tax advantage. According to Section 80E , the interest paid on an eligible education loan may be deducted from taxable income. There is no monetary limit on the eligible interest deduction, subject to the conditions of Section 80E, and the deduction can be claimed for up to eight assessment years. The deduction is available on the interest paid, not the principal repayment. It applies to both secured and unsecured education loans that meet the requirements of Section 80E. The person who obtains the loan and pays interest can claim the deduction. A parent who takes a loan for their children can also claim a deduction, subject to the applicable conditions. Because the tax rules can change, it is suggested to check the latest Income Tax Department provisions or consult a qualified tax professional before claiming the deduction. How to Apply for a Collateral-Free Education Loan If you are wondering how to get an education loan without collateral, follow these steps: Step 1: Check government schemes eligibility: Before applying for a collateral-free education loan abroad, check applicable government schemes and eligibility because these may reduce the borrowing cost. Step 2:Compare lenders: Compare the interest rates, maximum collateral-free amount, processing fees, moratorium period, and the repayment terms. Do not simply choose the loan with the lower interest rate. Step 3: Keep your documents ready: Keep your admission letter, school records, KYC papers, course fee details, and the co-applicant’s income and financial documents ready. Step 4: Apply with the lender: You can compare the available options and apply via the lender’s official website. Tata Capital Education Loan is an option you can consider to get a student loan without collateral. Step 5: Complete verification: The lender verifies the information and documents submitted with the application and assesses your eligibility under its lending criteria. Step 6: Review the sanction and disbursal: Once the loan has been approved, ensure you carefully check the approved amount, the interest rate, the fees, the moratorium, and the repayment terms. Once the necessary formalities have been completed, the loan will be disbursed to the institution’s fees. Conclusion An education loan without collateral may be used to pay for higher education without putting your property up as security. Eligible loans up to ₹7.5 lakh may receive government-backed guarantee support without collateral, whereas larger amounts depend on the lender, institution, course, and co-applicant’s profile. When considering studies abroad, you should carefully compare unsecured loans and check the government schemes before borrowing a loan. Also consider the interest that can accrue during the moratorium and whether you qualify for the Section 80E deduction. Tata Capital is one option to compare eligible students looking for collateral-free education financing. Disclaimer: This information is for general awareness only. Scheme limits, interest rates, eligibility criteria, and lender terms may change. Always verify the latest terms with the relevant government authority or lender before applying. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Are you curious about making your loans easier to handle? Imagine having superpowers that help you reduce the money you owe and save on extra charges. We’re about to uncover the secrets of part-payment, part-payment meaning, pre-payment, and pre-closure of loans. These are like magic tools that can make your loan journey smoother and save you some extra rupees. What is Part Payment of a Loan Part payment means paying a lump sum toward your loan in addition to your regular EMIs, without closing the loan. The amount goes directly toward reducing your outstanding principal. Since interest is charged on the principal, a lower balance brings down your total interest. Depending on your lender, you can either lower your EMI while keeping the tenure the same, or keep the EMI and shorten the tenure. You can usually make part payments more than once during the loan, subject to your lender’s rules. Advantages of Part-Payment Reduces your outstanding principal, which lowers the total interest you pay. Gives you the choice between a lower EMI and a shorter tenure. Can be done in multiple installments, making it a flexible way to use surplus funds. Has little to no negative effect on your credit score because the loan remains active and in good standing. Disadvantages of Part-Payment Part payment charges: Some lenders apply a fee on the amount you part-pay, depending on the loan type. For floating-rate loans taken for non-business purposes, RBI rules mean no such charges apply. Lock-in periods: Many lenders set a minimum period before you can make a part payment, or limit how often and how much you can pay in a year. Opportunity cost: Money used to make a partial payment is money you cannot use elsewhere. If your loan interest is low, those funds might earn more in another investment. Prepayment of a Loan Loan prepayment means repaying a large part of your loan, or the full outstanding amount, before the tenure ends. A partial payment covers only a portion of the balance, while a full prepayment settles the entire remaining balance. The main benefit is interest savings, since a lower or nil principal means less interest overall. Prepayment can also either reduce your EMI or shorten your tenure, depending on the option you choose. Some lenders apply a prepayment charge, and whether it applies depends on the lender and the type of loan . Always check your loan terms before you prepay. Advantages of Prepayment? Lowers the principal, which reduces the total interest you pay. Can shorten your tenure or reduce your EMI, based on your preference. Helps you become debt-free sooner and eases long-term repayment pressure. Timely prepayment can strengthen your credit profile over time. Disadvantages of Prepayment? Prepayment charges: A fee may apply, and it depends on the lender and loan type. For floating-rate loans taken for non-business purposes, RBI rules mean no prepayment charges apply. Reduced liquidity: Using a large sum to prepay can leave you with less cash for emergencies or other needs. Opportunity cost: The same funds could potentially earn more if invested elsewhere, especially when your loan rate is low. What is Loan Pre-Closure? Loan pre-closure means repaying your entire outstanding loan in one payment before the scheduled end of the tenure. Once you pre-close, your EMIs stop and the loan account is settled and closed. To pre-close, you apply to your lender, who calculates the final amount based on your outstanding principal and any applicable charges. After payment, collect a No Objection Certificate (NOC) confirming that all dues are cleared. Advantages of Pre-Closure? Ends your EMIs entirely and makes you debt-free ahead of schedule. Saves on the interest you would have paid over the remaining tenure. Credit score: Closing a loan successfully can strengthen your credit profile and reflects disciplined repayment. Disadvantages of Pre-Closure? Pre-closure charges: A fee may apply depending on the lender and loan type. For floating-rate loans taken for non-business purposes, RBI rules mean no pre-closure charges apply. Reduced liquidity: Paying off the full balance at once uses a large amount of cash that could otherwise be kept for emergencies. Lock-in period: Some lenders require you to complete a minimum period before you can pre-close the loan. Difference Between Part-Payment, Prepayment, and Pre-Closure Each option helps you repay your loan faster and save on interest, but they work in different ways. Part-payment clears a portion of your loan while it continues, prepayment clears a large part or all of it before term, and pre-closure settles the entire loan and closes the account. The table below compares them at a glance. Aspects Part-Payment of Loan Prepayment of Loan Pre-Closure of Loan Reduces Principal Amount Yes Yes Full Loan Repayment Effect on Interest Rate Stays the Same Interest Rate Goes Down Stays the Same Impact on EMI EMI Becomes Smaller EMI Becomes Smaller No More EMI Effect on Credit Rating Little to No Impact Can Improve Credit Score Can Improve Credit Score Frequency Can be done multiple times One-time or occasional One-time, closes the loan Charges May apply, subject to lender and loan type May apply, subject to lender and loan type May apply, subject to lender and loan type Loan Status Remains active Remains active Closed and settled Loan Prepayment Charges and Rules in India Depending on your lender, you may be charged a penalty ranging from 2% to 5% when you choose to make a prepayment of a loan before the scheduled date. For instance, Tata Capital levies loan pre-closure charges of 4.5% on amounts over and above 25% of your outstanding principal. To understand the exact amount you might need to pay, use tools like Tata Capital’s online loan prepayment calculator to estimate these charges easily. It’s also important to note that many lenders may limit prepayments and may have certain caps in place. How Each Option Impacts Your Credit Score Prepayment of a loan can positively impact your credit score in several ways. When you clear a loan early or reduce a large portion of your outstanding balance, your overall debt decreases. This lowers your credit utilisation ratio and displays disciplined repayment behaviour, which can make your credit profile stronger over time. Part-payment of loan, on the other hand, usually has a negligible effect. While they reduce the outstanding principal and future interest, the loan itself is still active. This means your EMI cycle continues as usual. Therefore, the impact on your credit score is limited. However, it still supports more manageable repayment and better long-term financial health. When to Choose Part Payment, Prepayment, or Pre-Closure When you’re choosing how to repay your loan, there is no single option that works for everyone. It is crucial to select the approach that aligns with your financial goals and situation. Consider factors such as your income stability, available surplus funds, and the remaining principal on your loan. For instance, if you have enough savings for a modest lump sum, a part-payment or prepayment of loan can lower your interest burden. However, if you’ve accumulated sufficient funds to clear the entire balance, opting for a loan pre-closure may be more beneficial. When not to Prepay a Loan Whether you should prepay your loan or not depends on several factors, including: 1. The stage of repayment you have currently reached 2. The interest rate on your loan 3. Any applicable loan pre-closure charges or prepayment charges Once you assess these factors, you can determine whether prepaying your loan aligns with your overall financial goals. Multiple Part Payments Rules You can make multiple part-payments toward your loan, gradually reducing the principal and cutting down the interest you pay in the long run. However, different lending institutions have their own rules for part-payments. These usually cover how much you’re allowed to part-pay at a time and how many times you can do it in a year. Documents Required for Loan Pre-Closure In order to initiate the loan pre-closure process, you must have the following documents in order: 1. Loan Account Number: This acts as your loan’s identification number and allows your bank to locate your specific loan account. 2. A Pre-closure Request: A formal letter indicating the borrower’s intent to pre-close the loan. 3. Your Photo ID: A valid government-issued identification (such as your Aadhaar card or Passport) for verification. 4. Your PAN Card: As with most financial procedures, a PAN card is required to initiate the pre-closure process. 5. Your Loan Documents: Your loan agreement, recent EMI statements, and any other related documents. 6. Your Payment Details: You must specify how you are closing the loan, such as through a demand draft, cheque, or another method. 7. An NOC from Lender: Obtained after loan closure, confirming that all dues have been settled. Summing Up – So, what’s the big picture? These loan tricks – part-payment, pre-payment, and pre-closure – help you handle your loans better. It’s like having secret weapons to make your loan journey smoother. You can reduce the amount you owe, pay less interest, and maybe even finish the loan game earlier. So, next time you’re thinking about small personal loans , consider these cool tricks to make your financial journey more awesome. Prepayment is like paying part of the loan early, while foreclosure is finishing the whole loan before its time. What happens in pre-closure in banking? Pre-closure in banking is when you pay off the entire loan before the time it is supposed to end. How does part prepayment reduce EMI? Part prepayment can make your EMI smaller or reduce the time you have to pay Does foreclosure affect your credit score? No, finishing your loan early (foreclosure) can make your credit score better. Can part prepayment reduce my credit score? Part prepayment usually doesn’t affect your credit score much. It can make paying off your loan easier. How does RBI regulate loan prepayment charges According to RBI regulations, borrowers with floating-rate loans for non-business purposes won’t face prepayment charges. For business loans, major lenders, such as commercial banks and large NBFCs, also cannot levy these fees. Smaller lenders, including regional rural banks and mid-sized NBFCs, are restricted from levying loan pre-closure charges on loans up to ₹50 lakh. What documents are required for loan pre-closure? The documents required for pre-closure of loan will depend on your lender. However, the records required will generally include the loan account number, a pre-closure request, a photo ID, your PAN card, any loan documents, payment details, and an NOC from your lender after closure. Can I make multiple part payments on my loan? You can usually make multiple part-payments on your loan, but the rules vary by lender. Always check your lender’s policies before making part payment of loan. When is it NOT advisable to prepay a loan? Deciding whether to prepay your loan depends on several factors, including how far you are into the repayment cycle, the current interest rate on your loan, and any applicable prepayment or loan pre-closure charges. Most of the time, these two terms come into play when wanting to reduce cash shortcomings and keep track of expected expenditures or sudden emergencies. Although they share the objective of facilitating access to capital, their conditions, intentions, and procedures vary considerably. Understanding when to select a loan versus an advance is crucial for efficiently managing significant investments, such as purchasing a home or addressing temporary financial shortfalls, thereby conserving time, reducing stress, and saving money. This guide will explore the essential features, advantages, and optimal applications of loans and advances, providing you with the knowledge to make informed financial decisions. What Are Loans? Loans are long-term financial agreements between lenders and borrowers. These are for large expenses or investments. They are usually repaid in installments over months or years. Common Uses of Loans Purchasing property (home loans) Financing higher education (education loans) Starting or expanding a business requires business loans. Consolidating debt (personal loans) Types of Loans Type Description Examples Secured Loans Collateral assets like property, gold, or investments are necessary. Lower interest rates apply. Home loans, gold loans Unsecured Loans No collateral is required. The lender’s increased risk leads to higher interest rates. Personal loans and credit cards Key Features of Loans Proof of income, credit report, and other financial documents form a long list. Interest rates vary depending on the kind of loan and lender policies. It is uncertain whether the collateral is necessary. The flexibility of loans makes them suitable for significant, planned expenses. What Are Advances? Advances are short-term credit facilities provided by financial institutions, employers, or lenders to meet immediate cash requirements. Advances are simpler, faster, and involve fewer formalities compared to loans. Common Uses of Advances Covering unexpected medical expenses Addressing mid-month cash crunches Ensure to settle bills or rent before the day of pay. Types of Advances Type Description Examples Salary Advances Employers offer this service to help employees cover urgent expenses before payday. Mid-month advances Hybrid Term Loan It permits individuals to borrow beyond their account balance up to a predetermined limit. Hybrid term loan facility. Bank overdrafts Cash Credit Provide short-term working capital against inventory or receivables. Business cash credits Payday Loans Instant loans cover expenses until the next paycheck. Kotak Payday Loans Key Features of Advances Repayment terms are usually weeks to months. Documentation is minimal, often consisting only of proof of income or employment. Interest Rates: lower than loans, and in some cases, interest-free (e.g., employer advances). Collateral: Rarely required. They are specifically designed to meet immediate, small-scale financial needs. The Difference between Loans and Advances Below is a detailed comparison: Feature Loans Advances Repayment Tenure Long-term (1 to 30 years) Short-term (weeks to months) Interest Rates The amount varies based on the creditworthiness and type of loan. This is especially true for employer salary advances. Collateral It’s required for secured loans but optional for unsecured ones. Rarely required Purpose You can use it for property, education, or business, making it versatile. Specific – short-term needs like medical emergencies Documentation The process is extensive, involving credit checks and financial statements. Minimal, often requiring proof of employment Processing Time The process is prolonged because of the documentation and approval procedures. Quick, sometimes instantaneous Risk for Lender The interest rate is lower for secured loans because of the collateral. Higher, as advances are often unsecured Loan Amount Larger amounts are required to cover significant financial needs. Smaller amounts are needed to address immediate cash requirements. Determine your financial stability and income to figure out if you can repay quickly or require long-term flexibility. Borrowing Cost: Compare the whole cost, including interest and fees. Advances may save money for short-term needs. Advances are faster and easier to get than loans if time is tight. Failure to repay loans or advance payments can hurt your credit score. Advantages of Loans and Advances Benefits of Loans Large Amounts: suitable for major expenses like property or education. Structured repayment is easier to manage with EMIs. A wide variety of options, tailored to specific needs such as home loans or business loans, are available. Benefits of Advances Quick Disbursal: Ideal for emergencies. Minimal Formalities: Easier to access with less documentation. Lower Interest Rates: They are often more affordable, especially for salary advances. Common Misconceptions About Loans and Advances Advances Are Always Better: While improvements are quick, they may not be sufficient for high-value needs. Loans are harder to obtain: With a favorable credit score and proper documentation, loan approval can be straightforward. Both are similar in that they are borrowing tools, but they cater to different financial requirements and timeframes. Choosing the Right Option Requirement Ideal Option Details Financing a family wedding Loans Covers high expenses with structured repayments, offering financial flexibility over time. Paying for urgent car repairs Advances Quick access to funds for immediate, smaller-scale needs like repairing a vehicle. Renovating a small portion of a home Advances Suitable for short-term, moderate expenses without the lengthy process of a loan. Expanding an existing business Loans Provides substantial capital required for scaling operations or investments in equipment. Covering a shortfall in monthly expenses Advances Addresses minor cash flow issues effectively until the next income cycle. Buying new office equipment Loans Ideal for significant, planned purchases with a repayment schedule to manage costs efficiently. Conclusion Advances and loans are highly valuable assets that serve a variety of financial purposes. While loans serve long-term, high-value investment plans, advances are ideal for short-term and urgent needs. It all depends on the purpose for which you want to use the funds, whether you have an immediate financial goal, your ability to repay the funds, the urgency of the needed funds, and whether you prefer short or long terms for the funds. An employer's short-term, temporary loan is known as a salary advance. It is generally interest-free. It has to be repaid in a month or two. A loan, on the other hand, is a formal borrowing from a financial institution and has a predetermined interest rate and repayment plan. What is the difference between a cash advance and a loan? A cash advance is a short-term borrowing with high interest rates and charges. These are generally made using a credit card. A loan, however, is a longer-term financial agreement with fixed payback terms and lower interest rates. Is it wise to make early loan payments? Paying off a loan early might save interest costs and speed up debt resolution. But before doing so, ensure that the lender hasn't imposed any penalties or hidden fees. Is salary advance good or bad? Salary advances are useful for short-term, interest-free financial demands, but they are not a long-term answer because they can cause financial strain and poor planning if used repeatedly. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Summary A loan repayment schedule is a detailed timetable indicating how and when you must repay the borrowed money. It lists the due dates and payment amounts, and breaks down the principal and interest for each payment. It also mentions the remaining loan amount after you make your payment. After referring to the payment schedule, you can plan your monthly budget and see how much total interest you will pay over time. The schedule also helps you stay on track to avoid late fees. A loan repayment schedule provides a structured plan outlining how you will repay the borrowedamount over a specific period. When a lender approves a loan, it provides a loan repayment schedule, listing every Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) you need to pay over the loan tenure. The schedule shows both the principal and interest component. This guide explains what a loan repayment schedule is, what it includes, how it is calculated, and how you can use it to manage your loan effectively. What is a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule, or a payment schedule, meaning the document lenders provide when your loan is approved is a table with all the necessary loan repayment details. It clearly shows every EMI from start to finish, the interest charged, how much you still owe, and when your loan will be fully repaid. It makes financial planning much easier and saves you from surprises later. What does a loan repayment schedule contain? The components of a loan repayment schedule are as follows: Component Meaning EMI number The sequence of each monthly payment. EMI due date The date on which you need to pay EMI. EMI amount The total amount you pay every month. Principal component The portion of the EMI that reduces your loan amount. Interest component The portion of the EMI charged as interest by the lender. Outstanding principal balance The remaining loan amount after each EMI is paid. In a standard reducing-balance loan, the interest component is higher in the initial EMIs because it is calculated on a larger outstanding principal. As you repay the loan, the principal balance decreases, so the interest portion reduces while the principal component gradually increases. How is a loan repayment schedule calculated? To calculate the loan repayment schedule, most lenders use the reducing-balance (amortization) method. Here, monthly interest is calculated on the outstanding principal, and the remaining portion of the EMI is applied to reduce the principal. Since the outstanding balance decreases with each payment, the interest charged on the next EMI is lower. To calculate EMI, you can use the formula given below: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1) Where, P = principal loan amount r = monthly interest rate n = loan tenure (in months) Here’s an illustrative example for better understanding. Suppose you borrow Rs. 5 lakh for 5 years at an interest rate of 10% per annum. You will have a fixed EMI of Rs. 10,624, and a total interest payout of Rs. 1,37,411. The first few EMIs will contain more interest than principal. Gradually, the interest portion will decrease while the principal repayment will increase. You can use an online EMI calculator to instantly generate a detailed payment schedule. Also Read – Loan vs. Advance What is the importance of a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule is important for several reasons, such as: Planning your budget: You can track EMI amounts and due dates. Knowing your interest cost: It shows the total interest payable over the loan tenure. Deciding on prepayments: You can estimate potential interest savings. Planning taxes: It helps you keep track of eligible tax benefits on the loan. Comparing loans: You can evaluate different loan offers based on the total repayment cost. How to get your loan repayment schedule? Your lender usually provides a loan repayment schedule when the loan is disbursed. You can also download it at any time through your online loan account or customer portal. If you are planning a new loan, use Tata Capital’s EMI Calculator to estimate your repayment schedule and manage your loan with confidence. What are the tips to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively? If you want to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively, here are some helpful tips: Set up auto-debit: Enable NACH or auto-debit to avoid missing EMI payments. Check before prepaying: Review your schedule to estimate possible interest savings. Request an updated schedule: Ask your lender for a revised schedule if your floating interest rate changes. Track principal repayments: Keep a record of the principal repaid each year for home loan tax filing purposes. Also Read – What is Part-Payment, Pre-Payment, Pre-Closure of Loan? Conclusion A loan repayment schedule is an important financial planning tool that shows how each EMI is divided between principal and interest. It helps you manage your cash flow and make informed prepayment decisions. The actual repayment schedule depends on your loan amount, interest rate, and tenure, and thus, do not refer to the standard ones available online. A loan repayment schedule is a table that includes the EMI amount, payment dates, principal repaid, interest charged, and the remaining loan balance after each payment. How is a loan repayment schedule calculated? A loan repayment schedule is calculated using the loan amount, interest rate, loan tenure, and EMI amount. It shows how every EMI is split between principal and interest until the loan is fully repaid. What is the difference between the principal and interest component in an EMI? The principal is the original loan amount you borrow, while the interest is the cost of borrowing that money. Can I get my loan repayment schedule online? Yes. Most banks and lenders allow you to download your loan repayment schedule through their website, mobile app, or internet banking portal. Does a repayment schedule change on a floating rate loan? Yes. A loan repayment schedule may change if the interest rate increases or decreases. The EMI amount, loan tenure, or both may be revised to reflect the new interest rate. NBFCs and authorised platforms using Aadhaar or other verified personal details. Identity verification is still required, and a no-PAN check may not capture your complete credit history. If your PAN is available, using it can help match your credit accounts more accurately You can check CIBIL score without PAN card using Aadhaar, your name, date of birth and registered mobile number, or through your bank/NBFC app, depending on the platform. However, you will still need to verify your identity, usually through an OTP or another authentication method. A no-PAN check may not show your complete credit history because credit accounts are commonly linked to your PAN. Websites promising a “no PAN, no OTP” CIBIL check should be treated as unsafe. This article explains the legitimate ways to check your CIBIL score without a PAN card, why identity verification is still required, how to check your score using PAN when it is available, and what to look for when avoiding fraudulent credit-score websites. Can You Really Check a CIBIL Score Without a PAN Card? Yes. The available method depends on the platform. However, PAN does remain an important identifier because lenders commonly report it with your loan and credit card information. It therefore helps the credit bureau match different credit accounts to the correct person. Without a valid PAN, the platform may still identify you through other information, but some accounts may not be matched. Make sure to check which ID options the platform accepts before starting. Ways to Check Your CIBIL Score Without a PAN Card You can check your CIBIL score without a PAN card through certain banks, NBFCs and authorised platforms using Aadhaar, another accepted ID or verified personal details. 1. Through Your Bank or NBFC App Some banks and NBFCs provide a credit score or credit-health feature within their app or internet banking service. To check: Log in through the official app or website. Look for the credit score or credit health section. Follow the instructions shown on screen. Complete any additional authentication requested. View your available score. If you are already verified within the app, the provider may not ask for PAN or a fresh OTP again. The process varies by provider. 2. Using Aadhaar or Another Accepted ID Some authorised financial platforms may allow Aadhaar or another accepted identity document to verify you. The process may involve: Selecting the available ID type. Entering the corresponding ID number. Providing your name, date of birth and contact details. Completing OTP or another required authentication step. Viewing the score if the platform can match your credit profile.. 3. Using Your Name, Date of Birth and Mobile Number Some platforms may first try to locate your credit profile using details such as your full name, date of birth and mobile number. This route still requires identity verification and may not retrieve every PAN-linked account. The platform may ask for an accepted ID or PAN if it cannot establish an accurate match. If you have access to your PAN, using it can make it easier to match the credit accounts reported against your profile. Why You Usually Still Need OTP (and Why That’s a Good Thing) You usually need an OTP because your identity must be verified before your CIBIL information can be released. This protects you from someone using your PAN or other personal details to access your credit report without your permission. A legitimate consumer service cannot give you your CIBIL score with no identity verification at all. If you search for checking CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP, be cautious of websites promising a “PAN only, no OTP” check. A request for your PAN alone should not be enough to access your credit information. OTP is a security measure and not an unnecessary friction. It helps confirm that you are the person requesting access to your credit information. You may not always receive a fresh OTP if you have already been authenticated through your bank or financial app, but some form of identity verification is still required. If a website promises to show your CIBIL score without OTP or any other verification, treat it as a red flag and avoid sharing your personal or financial information. How to Spot Fake ‘Free CIBIL Check’ Websites You can spot a fake CIBIL check website by checking whether it uses proper identity verification, protects your financial information and clearly explains how it handles your data. A legitimate check may ask for your PAN or another accepted ID, mobile number and OTP or another form of identity verification. Warning signs include: No identity verification: Be cautious if a site promises your credit report without verifying who you are. Requests for banking credentials: A credit score check should not require your debit or credit card PIN, CVV, UPI PIN or net-banking password. Requests to share an OTP: Never tell an OTP to someone over a call, email or message. Suspicious website addresses: Check for spelling changes or domains designed to resemble a recognised financial institution. No clear privacy information: Avoid sites that do not explain how they collect and use your personal information. Misleading payment requests: CIBIL currently provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year. Note : If you become a victim of financial cyber fraud, report it through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal or call 1930. Checking Your CIBIL Score With a PAN Card (The Standard Way) If you have your PAN, it can make it easier to match the credit accounts reported under your name. To check your CIBIL score by PAN card, you can: Visit the official CIBIL platform or an authorised provider. Choose the option for a CIBIL Score and Report. Enter your PAN, name, date of birth and mobile number. Complete the required OTP or other identity verification. View your available score and credit report. Make sure the details you enter match your official records so the correct credit profile can be identified. Under RBI rules, you are entitled to one free full credit report, including your credit score, in a calendar year after due authentication. CIBIL also provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year, while banks, NBFCs and other authorised platforms may offer free periodic checks depending on their current services. Also Read – What is the maximum CIBIL score What You’ll Need and What It Means for Your Score To check your CIBIL score, you generally need an accepted ID such as PAN or Aadhaar, your registered mobile number for authentication, and basic personal details such as your name and date of birth. You may also need: Email address, if required by the platform Access to the required authentication method, such as OTP Since it is a self-check and not a lender enquiry made when you apply for credit, checking your own CIBIL score causes zero impact on your score. Understanding the CIBIL score range can help you analyse what each number indicates. If you check your score without PAN and an account appears to be missing, cross-check your credit report using PAN when it is available. A PAN-based check may help match accounts that were not identified through the no-PAN route. Also Read – Will a Loan Settlement Ruin My CIBIL Score Conclusion You can check your CIBIL score without a PAN card through NBFCs or authorised platforms using Aadhaar, another accepted ID or verified personal details. However, identity verification is still required, and a no-PAN check may not always show your complete credit history. If you have your PAN, using it can make it easier to match your credit accounts. Avoid unfamiliar websites promising to check CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP and no other verification. Credit scores and reports are issued by TransUnion CIBIL. Processes and availability may change, so use only official or authorised channels. If you suspect financial cyber fraud, report it through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. FAQs Can I check my CIBIL score without a PAN card? Yes. If you want to know how to check CIBIL score without a PAN card, some platforms may accept Aadhaar, another permitted ID or verified personal details. Your bank or NBFC may also provide access to your credit score, depending on the service available and the verification process it follows. Can I check my CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP? No. You will still need to verify your identity. If you are already logged in to your bank or financial app, a separate OTP may not be needed. Be careful with websites that say you can check CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP or any verification. How do I check my CIBIL score with my PAN card? To check CIBIL score by PAN card, use the official CIBIL platform or an authorised provider. Enter your PAN, name, date of birth and contact details, then complete the required verification. When you check CIBIL score using a PAN card, make sure the information matches your official records so the correct credit profile can be identified. Is it safe to check my CIBIL score on third-party websites? Yes, but only if the platform is recognised and follows proper security and authentication practices. Avoid websites asking for your card PIN, CVV, UPI PIN or net-banking password. Also check whether the site clearly explains how it uses your data and whether it requires proper identity verification before showing your credit information. Does checking my own CIBIL score lower it? No. Checking your own CIBIL score does not lower it. It is treated as a self-check rather than a lender enquiry made for a new credit application. Will a check without PAN show my full credit history? Not always. Some accounts may not show up without your PAN. If your report looks incomplete, check it again using your PAN when possible. How often can I check my CIBIL score for free? CIBIL currently provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year. RBI rules also provide for one free full credit report, including the credit score, in each calendar year after due authentication. Additional checks may be available through banks, NBFCs or authorised platforms, depending on their current service and access policy. need to maintain your desired lifestyle after you stop working. Your age, income, risk appetite, liquidity needs and tax situation can then help determine how NPS, EPF, PPF, mutual funds and pension plans fit into your retirement strategy. Looking for the best retirement plan in India starts with the amount you may need after retirement rather than a product name. A pension plan, NPS, EPF, PPF or mutual fund can each play a different role depending on your age, income, risk appetite and need for liquidity. In fact, your tax regime also affects which options may suit you. For income earned from 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies and the new tax regime remains the default, although taxpayers can opt for the old regime where permitted. Employer contributions to NPS remain an important exception. The same option can therefore work differently for two people with similar retirement goals. Your corpus target, time to retirement, ability to take risk and need for access to the money should determine how you combine the available options. This guide compares the main retirement-planning categories rather than ranking individual branded products as the “best” choice. How Much Do You Need to Retire? First estimate how much annual income you may need after retirement. Start with your current household expenses, remove costs that may end before retirement and add expenses that could rise later, particularly healthcare. Then account for inflation until your expected retirement age. For example, suppose your household expenses are ₹6 lakh a year today and you plan to retire in 20 years. At an assumed inflation rate of 6% a year, the same level of spending would be about ₹19.2 lakh annually by then. Next, estimate how long the corpus may need to last and factor in any pension, rent or other regular income you expect to receive. A retirement calculator can combine your age, existing savings, expected expenses, inflation and return assumptions to estimate the gap. Once you know the target corpus and any shortfall, you can decide how to allocate your retirement savings across pension schemes, provident funds and market-linked investments. Main Retirement Planning Options in India To begin with the major options, note that NPS, PPF, mutual funds , EPF, annuities and SCSS do not serve the same purpose. Their risk, liquidity, tax treatment and income structure are different. NPS and mutual funds are market-linked, while EPF, PPF and SCSS follow different government-backed structures. Insurer pension products may provide more predictable income but can offer less flexibility. These differences matter more than choosing a product simply because it is presented as the best pension plan in India. Retirement Planning and the New Tax Regime: What Changed For Tax Year 2026-27, which covers income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies. The new tax regime continues as the default regime, while taxpayers who are eligible can opt for the old regime. Under the new regime, many personal deductions that influenced retirement-product choices under the old regime are no longer available. The deduction corresponding to the old Section 80C is now provided under Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The ₹1.5 lakh aggregate deduction remains in the new Act, but Section 123 is not available under the new concessional tax regime . NPS : NPS (National Pension System) is a market-linked pension scheme in India regulated by PFRDA. Contributions can be allocated across permitted asset classes and returns depend on the performance of the underlying investments. Under the current PFRDA framework for the All Citizen Model, a normal exit can allow up to 80% of the accumulated corpus as a lump sum, with at least 20% used to purchase an annuity, subject to applicable conditions and corpus thresholds. This 80/20 structure applies to the current All Citizen Model, so it should not be replaced with the older 60/40 figure without specifying the NPS model. The withdrawal limit and tax exemption are not the same. Current income-tax rules provide exemption for up to 60% of the NPS corpus on final lump-sum withdrawal, while pension received from an annuity is taxable. EPF : Employee Provident Fund (EPF) is employment-linked and receives employee and employer contributions. Subject to applicable conditions, EPF generally follows an EEE structure, meaning qualifying contributions, interest and withdrawals receive tax benefits. PPF : Public Provident Fund (PPF) is government-backed with a 15-year term. Interest and qualifying maturity proceeds are tax-free, while its contribution deduction mainly benefits old-regime taxpayers. Annuity and Pension Plans from Insurers: How to Evaluate Them An insurance pension plan usually involves paying premiums over time or investing a lump sum to receive retirement income later. An immediate annuity starts payouts soon after purchase, while a deferred arrangement begins at a future date. The pension amount alone does not tell you whether an annuity is suitable. Check for: Annuity Rate: Compare the income offered against the amount invested. Payout Structure: Check whether payments continue for one life, joint lives or include return of purchase price. Charges: Review costs that may apply during accumulation, withdrawal or surrender. Liquidity: Check whether and when the invested amount can be accessed. Inflation Impact: A fixed pension can lose purchasing power over a long retirement. Insurer Record: Review relevant financial strength, servicing and claims information. Tax Treatment: Check how contributions, maturity proceeds and pension income are taxed. Annuity rates can be modest compared with the growth potential of market-linked assets over long periods and surrender terms can be restrictive. The trade-off is greater certainty of income when comparing pension plans in India. Also read – What is Net Asset Value How to Build Your Retirement Plan: A Simple Framework A retirement corpus is usually built from more than one source. The mix can be planned around 5 factors: Define the Corpus Goal: Estimate future living, healthcare and other retirement costs after inflation, then calculate how much you may need to accumulate. Use Different Options for Different Needs: EPF or PPF may add stability, mutual funds can provide market-linked growth, NPS can bring structure to retirement investing and an annuity may help create predictable income. Check Your Tax Regime: Do not assume an investment carries the same deduction under both regimes. If your employer contributes to NPS, check whether the available deduction applies to you. Increase Contributions as Income Grows: A contribution fixed early in your career may become too small as income and expenses rise. Increasing it periodically can help keep the corpus target within reach. Review the Plan Regularly: Recalculate the requirement when your income, expenses, retirement age, investment performance or tax rules change. When comparing the best retirement plans, assess the overall mix against your time horizon, risk capacity, liquidity requirements and expected retirement income. For individual investment decisions, consider consulting a SEBI-registered investment adviser. Common Retirement Planning Mistakes Retirement plans often fall short because people start late, underestimate future costs or rely too heavily on one investment. Common mistakes include: Buying Mainly for a Tax Deduction: A deduction available under the old regime may not apply under the new regime. Depending on One Instrument: A single option may not provide enough growth, liquidity and income flexibility. Ignoring Inflation: The amount needed to maintain today’s lifestyle can rise considerably by retirement. Starting Too Late: A shorter accumulation period can require substantially higher contributions. Underestimating Healthcare Costs: Medical spending can become a larger part of the household budget later in life. Ignoring NPS Annuity Taxation: Pension received from the annuity portion is taxable under current rules. Not Reviewing the Plan: Tax rules, pension regulations and personal circumstances can change. Also read – What is the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)? Conclusion A retirement plan should show how much money you need, where that money will come from and how each investment supports that goal. NPS can add market-linked retirement savings, EPF and PPF can provide stability, mutual funds can support long-term growth and annuities can create regular income after retirement. The mix should be reviewed as your income, expenses, retirement age or tax position changes. That is more useful than choosing a product mainly for a deduction or advertised return. There is no single best retirement plan in India for everyone. The suitable mix depends on your retirement corpus, age, income, risk tolerance, liquidity needs and tax regime. The right choice depends on how much growth, stability, liquidity and retirement income you need. What is the difference between a pension plan and NPS? A pension plan from an insurer generally provides retirement benefits or annuity income according to its policy terms. NPS is a PFRDA-regulated and a market-linked retirement system. They differ in investment structure, liquidity, charges, exit rules, tax treatment and the way retirement income is generated. Do pension plans still give a tax benefit under the new regime? Not necessarily. Many personal deductions associated with retirement investments are not available under the new regime. Eligible employer NPS contributions remain an important exception. Check the current tax treatment of the specific investment rather than assuming a pension product automatically provides a deduction. How much should I invest for retirement in India? There is no fixed amount or percentage for everyone. Estimate your future expenses after inflation, calculate the corpus required and subtract existing retirement savings and expected income. Your age, years until retirement, risk level and expected investment performance will influence the contribution required. What are the government pension schemes in India? NPS is a major government-regulated pension scheme in India. Other retirement-related arrangements include the Atal Pension Yojana and, for eligible government employees, the Unified Pension Scheme. EPF, PPF and SCSS are also widely used for retirement savings, although they do not all operate as pension schemes in the same way. Is NPS better than an insurance pension plan? Not necessarily. NPS is market-linked, while an insurance pension plan may offer guaranteed or defined income depending on the policy. The better option depends on whether you prioritise growth potential, predictable income, access to your money and the costs involved. When should I start retirement planning Start earlier as it gives your contributions more time to compound. If you begin later, the amount required each month may be higher to reach the same corpus. At any age, start by calculating the gap between your existing retirement savings and the amount you expect to need. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund EMI (Equated Monthly Instalment) is the fixed amount you pay every month towards your loan, which includes both the principal and the interest. It’s important to calculate your EMI so you can manage your budget and plan your finances effectively. You might think that calculating your EMI is tough, but it’s actually easy. With the EMI calculation formula in Excel, you can quickly determine your monthly payment without any hassle. In this article, we’ll walk you through every step of how to use the Excel formula and discuss the benefits of using it. What is EMI (Equated Monthly Instalment)? An EMI (Equated Monthly Instalment) is made up of two main components: the principal amount and the interest. It’s a fixed monthly payment that helps you manage your loan repayments effectively. To calculate your EMI using Excel, you’ll need the loan amount, interest rate, and loan tenure. With this information, Excel’s PMT function can quickly help you calculate your EMI, making it easier to plan and manage your loan payments throughout the tenure. EMI Calculation Formula in Excel Sheet (PMT Function) EMI stands for Equated Monthly Instalment. It’s the fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan. You can easily calculate your EMI in Excel using the PMT formula. The standard formula is: =PMT (rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type]) Key Components of the EMI Calculation in Excel Rate : This is the interest rate per period. For monthly EMI, divide the annual interest rate by 12. NPER (Number of Periods) : This is the total number of EMIs you’ll pay, usually the loan tenure in months. PV (Present Value) : This is the principal loan amount. Enter it as a negative number in the formula. FV (Future Value) : This is optional and usually set to 0. It represents the remaining loan balance at the end. TYPE : Enter 0 if EMI is paid at the end of the month, and 1 if it’s paid at the beginning. For example, if you take a loan of Rs. 5 lakh at 14.60% annual interest for 48 months, the formula will look like this: =PMT (0.01216666, 48, 500000, 0, 0) This gives you the exact EMI amount, Rs. 13,814. When calculating EMI, Excel helps you: Save time compared to manual calculations Avoid errors and get accurate results Plan your repayments efficiently Compare different loan offers easily Make financial planning more reliable and faster Step-by-Step EMI Calculation in Excel Using Formula You can easily calculate your EMI using Excel’s built-in PMT function, which simplifies the process and gives accurate results. Let’s say you’ve taken a Rs. 6,00,000 loan at an annual interest rate of 11.50% for a tenure of 2 years (24 months). Follow these steps: Step 1 : Open Excel and select an empty cell. Step 2 : Type the formula: =PMT ( Step 3 : Enter the monthly interest rate. Since the annual rate is 11.50%, divide it by 12: 11.50% / 12 = 0.958% or 0.00958 Type: 0.00958, Step 4 : Add a comma and enter the number of months. Since the loan tenure is 2 years, type: 24, Step 5 : Add another comma and enter the loan amount: 600000 Step 6 : Close the formula with a bracket and hit Enter. Excel will immediately calculate and show the EMI as approximately Rs. 28,103. Factors that affect the EMI amount Some factors that can influence your EMI amount are: Loan Amount : A higher loan amount results in a higher EMI, as you need to repay more. Interest Rate : A higher interest rate increases the EMI. Even a small change in the rate can have a significant impact. Loan Tenure : A longer tenure lowers the EMI amount but increases the total interest paid over time. A shorter tenure increases the EMI but reduces the overall interest. Prepayment or Part Payment : Making extra payments can reduce the loan balance, which in turn reduces the EMI or loan tenure. Type of Interest : Fixed interest rates result in a constant EMI throughout the tenure, while variable rates can cause fluctuations. Interest Calculation Method : The way interest is calculated affects the total loan cost. Loans with a reducing balance method generally cost less than those using a flat interest rate, even if the quoted rate is the same. Fees and Charges : Processing fees, documentation charges, and taxes increase the overall borrowing cost. Consider these charges along with the interest rate when comparing loan offers. Benefits of Online Emi Calculator vs Excel Emi Loan Calculator Both tools calculate the same EMI, but they serve different needs. An online EMI calculator is built for speed and simplicity, while an Excel EMI calculator gives you control and depth. Here is how the two compare. Online EMI Calculator An online EMI calculator asks for three inputs: the loan amount, the interest rate, and the tenure. It returns your monthly installment, total interest outgo, and total repayment in seconds, with no formulas to write and no scope for data entry errors in the calculation itself. Its biggest advantage is accessibility. You do not need any spreadsheet knowledge, and the results are instant, making it ideal for quickly comparing multiple loan offers or checking how a different tenure affects your EMI while you are still shortlisting lenders. For a fast, reliable answer to “what will my EMI be,” the online calculator is the tool to reach for. Excel EMI Calculator An Excel EMI calculator uses the PMT function to produce the same result, but its strength is what you can build around it. You can create a full amortization schedule showing the interest and principal split of every installment, model prepayments, simulate interest rate changes on floating-rate loans, and save multiple scenarios side by side in one file. The trade-off is that accuracy depends on you. The annual rate must be converted to a monthly rate, cell references must be correct, and the inputs need to be maintained as your loan changes. Excel suits borrowers who want to analyze and track a loan through its life, not just check an EMI once. Why Should You Calculate Your EMIs in Advance? One of the main reasons you should calculate your EMI in advance is that it helps you plan your monthly budget with ease. But that’s not the only reason. Here are a few more reasons why you should do it- It allows you to set aside the right amount for repayments without affecting other expenses. It helps you choose a loan amount that matches your financial capacity. It lets you compare loan options from different lenders based on EMI amounts. It gives you clarity on how the loan tenure impacts your monthly payments. It allows you to choose between a shorter or longer tenure depending on your goals. It helps you avoid any surprises during the repayment period. It helps you stay financially prepared and confident throughout the repayment journey. Advanced EMI Calculation in Excel: Building an Amortization Schedule You can also build an amortization schedule while performing calculation of EMI in Excel sheet for clearer loan tracking. When building an amortization schedule in Excel, first calculate your fixed monthly payment with the built-in PMT function: =PMT (rate, nper, pv), where the rate is the period-interest, “nper” the total number of payments and “pv” the loan amount. Next, lay out the monthly columns for interest, principal and remaining balance so you can clearly see the EMI breakup in Excel. The columns should indicate how much goes to interest and how much reduces principal each month. Finally use these same columns to create the full loan repayment schedule in Excel, showing each payment date, total EMI, interest portion, principal portion and outstanding balance until full repayment. Example amortization table based on EMI calculation in Excel format: Consider a loan of Rs. 6,00,000 at 10% annual interest, which equals 0.8333% per month, for a tenure of 12 months. How can I ensure the accuracy of EMI calculations using Excel? Start by carefully entering the correct loan amount, interest rate, and tenure. Why is the interest rate significant in EMI calculations? The interest rate directly affects how much you pay each month. Even a slight change in rate can make a noticeable difference in your EMI and the total cost of your loan, so it plays a key role in planning your finances. Why is it important to include additional charges when calculating EMI? Processing fees or other charges increase your effective loan amount. Ignoring them can lead to an inaccurate EMI figure and poor budgeting, so it’s smart to factor them in from the start. How does the loan tenure affect EMI calculations? A longer loan tenure spreads the repayment over more months, which lowers the EMI but increases the total interest paid. A shorter tenure means higher EMIs, but less interest in the long run.
