institution that you do not need to back with property or assets. Weddings, travel bookings, gifting and home upgrades tend to cluster into the same few weeks each year. When those expenses arrive before your next bonus or a fresh round of savings, a festive season personal loan can help bridge the gap. But borrowing for festive expenses needs careful planning. This article covers when a personal loan may make sense, what its benefits are, how eligibility works and what to consider before applying. Why consider a personal loan during the festive season? Festive expenses rarely spread out evenly, and most households feel the squeeze in the same few weeks, well before the next salary increment or bonus arrives. A festive season personal loan can help bridge this gap without requiring you to dip into long-term savings. This can be particularly useful when several planned expenses fall within a short period. Other reasons to opt for a personal loan include: It is unsecured, so no property, gold or investment needs to be pledged. Disbursal is fast enough to match tight festive timelines, whether that is a wedding date or a travel booking. The end-use is unrestricted, so a single loan can cover gifts, travel, a family function or a big-ticket purchase. Repayment is structured into fixed monthly installments, easier to plan around than ad hoc borrowing. Check – Documents Required for Personal Loan Key benefits of a festive personal loan The benefits of a festive season personal loan largely come down to flexibility, speed and convenience: It is a collateral-free festive loanthat puts no asset at risk for what is ultimately a discretionary, short-term expense. Since it is a flexible EMI festive loan, you can spread the cost over a tenure that suits your monthly budget, instead of draining savings in one go. A personal loan with quick approval for festive season expenses can be useful when you are working with fixed timelines, such as travel dates or family functions. The application process is also relatively straightforward, typically requiring basic KYC, identity and income documents. These advantages of a festive personal loan can make it a convenient option for families that need to manage planned expenses without depleting their savings at once. What can you use a festive personal loan for? A festive season personal loan is unrestricted in its end-use, unlike financing tied to a single purchase. This is one of the practical advantages of a festive personal loan compared with product-specific financing. Common uses include: Festival shopping and gifting Home renovation or new appliances before guests arrive Travel to visit family Funding a wedding Consolidating existing high-cost dues before the season begins Check – Personal Loan Interest Rates Eligibility and how to apply Basic eligibility criteria cover age, income, employment type and credit score, though specifics vary by offer. Personal loan eligibility for festive offers can change with each season, so it is worth checking the current criteria before you begin your application. Applying follows a short, predictable path. Check your personal loan eligibility for festive offers using the eligibility calculator. Fill in your personal, income and employment details. Upload the required KYC and income documents. Get your application reviewed and receive an approval decision. Once approved, the loan amount is disbursed to your bank account. The EMI calculator on the Tata Capital Personal Loan page can also help you estimate your monthly outgo before you apply. Festive personal loan vs credit card vs no-cost EMI Festive spending does not always call for the same financing option. Here’s how three common financing options compare: Option Best suited for Key consideration Personal loan Spread-out or larger festive spends Fixed, disclosed EMI Credit card Small, short-term purchases repaid quickly Revolving interest if not repaid in full No-cost EMI A single big purchase at a partner merchant Cost is often built into the price Borrow responsibly this festive season Festive spending is usually discretionary, so borrowing should be based on repayment capacity rather than the amount you are eligible to receive. Responsible borrowing is what separates a useful and flexible EMI festive loan from debt that adds financial pressure later. Borrow only what you can repay comfortably within your monthly budget. Avoid borrowing for consumption you would not otherwise be able to afford. Check the total cost, meaning interest plus fees, via the Key Facts Statement rather than the EMI alone. Do not stack multiple festive loans or buy-now-pay-later lines at the same time. Keep your EMI within a manageable share of your monthly income. A lender that spells this out clearly is one worth trusting; one that only sells the ease of borrowing usually is not. Conclusion A festive season personal loan can smooth front-loaded festive costs without pledging any asset. Its main strengths are speed, flexibility and collateral-free access. The best reason to opt for a personal loan is when you borrow only what comfortably fits your EMI. For the best festive offers, choose a Tata Capital Personal Loan . Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Interest rates differ based on how they are set and how interest is calculated. Common types include fixed, floating, hybrid, repo-linked , MCLR-linked, simple, compound, flat, and reducing balance rates. Understanding how each works can help borrowers compare EMIs, total borrowing costs, and repayment structures. Factors such as benchmarks, calculation methods, compounding, and APR can significantly affect the actual cost of a loan. The main types of interest rate differ in two ways: how the rate is set and how interest is calculated. A rate may be fixed, floating, or linked to a benchmark such as the repo rate. Separately, interest may use the simple, compound, flat, or reducing balance method. Both choices affect the EMI and total borrowing cost. This guide explains the different types of interest rates in India and helps you compare their costs clearly before selecting a borrowing product. The types of interest rates on loans show how a rate is set and how interest is calculated. Types of interest rates at a glance So, how many types of interest rates are there? The table below covers nine common categories. Basis Type Meaning Rate setting Fixed Remains constant Floating Follows a benchmark Hybrid/dual Fixed, then floating Repo-linked/ External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) Follows approved external benchmark (usually repo rate) Marginal Cost of Funds-Based Lending Rate (MCLR) Follows bank’s internal benchmark Calculation Simple Calculated on principal only Compound Calculated on principal plus accrued interest Flat Calculated based on the original principal Reducing balance Calculated based on the outstanding principal Fixed vs floating interest rate Fixed rates offer predictable EMIs, but may start higher and include prepayment charges. On the other hand, floating rates track a benchmark which affects the EMI or tenure. RBI directions bar prepayment charges for floating, non-business individual loans sanctioned or renewed from January 1, 2026. Fixed-rate charges depend on the contract. For borrowers who want a middle path, a hybrid interest rate starts fixed, then floats. Choosing between fixed, floating, and hybrid interest rates depends on how much uncertainty in EMIs and tenure you are comfortable with. Different types of interest rates suit individuals with various levels of risk tolerance, so it’s always wise to compare the types of interest rates on loans and check the relevant benchmark before making a decision. Repo-linked and EBLR rates: How floating rates work in India Since October 2019, RBI has required banks to link new floating-rate retail loans to an external benchmark under the EBLR framework. The different types of interest rates in India under EBLR can track various benchmarks like the repo rate (repo-linked rate), specified Treasury bill yields, or another approved benchmark. The total interest rate on a floating loan equals the benchmark plus the lender’s spread, and resets at least every three months. For instance, the present repo rate is 5.25% as of August 5, 2026 . If the RBI changes the repo rate later, the revised rate must be reflected in eligible EBLR-linked loans within the three-month reset cycle. EBLR transmits policy changes faster than MCLR, which is an internal lending benchmark based on a bank’s marginal cost of funds, and only applies to some older loans. The types of interest rate risks for an MCLR-linked loan include a higher EMI or longer tenure when the benchmark rises. Simple vs compound interest While simple interest uses principal only, compound interest also uses accumulated interest. Here’s an example of how these two different types of interest rates work: At 10% over two years, ₹1 lakh incurs ₹20,000 simple interest or ₹21,000 with annual compounding. Simple interest usually appears in some short-tenure products, while compounding is more common in investments and long loans. Flat vs reducing balance interest With a flat rate, interest is calculated on the full loan amount throughout the tenure, even as you repay it. On the other hand, with a reducing rate , interest is calculated only on the amount you still owe. Therefore, when comparing types of interest rates on loans, it’s so important to check the total repayment amount, as two loans quoting the same interest rate can have different costs depending on whether they use the flat or reducing balance method. Nominal vs effective interest rate (and APR) The nominal interest rate is the stated rate, without accounting for compounding or fees, excluding compounding and fees. On the other hand, the effective rate includes compounding. What this means is that if a 12% nominal rate is compounded monthly, after interest is added every month, the effective annual rate increases to approximately 12.68%. The Annual Percentage Rate (APR) combines loan interest and associated charges. RBI requires its computation in the Key Facts Statement before a retail term-loan contract is executed. When comparing types of loans and interest rates, use APR because a low flat rate may conceal a high effective cost. Which type of loan has the highest interest rate? Secured home, gold, and auto loans cost less because the collateral reduces risk. Unsecured personal loans cost more, while revolving credit-card debt and informal or dealer flat-rate finance are often the most expensive. However, always remember that your interest rate is also highly dependent on your borrowing profile and chosen lender. Conclusion Understanding the various types of interest rates requires checking rate setting and calculation. When you understand the various terms related to loans and know how to compare them based on APR, you become empowered to choose the right credit option for your needs. For a smooth loan application process, explore a Tata Capital Personal Loan . Do note that the rates, benchmarks, and terms may change at the RBI’s or lender’s discretion. All this is general information only, and it is essential to always compare the different types of interest rates available in India before choosing. While fixed interest rates stay constant, floating interest rates follow a benchmark and may change the repayment amount with fluctuations. What is a repo-linked or EBLR interest rate? An EBLR interest rate follows an approved external benchmark, and is commonly repo-linked since it follows the RBI’s repo rate. What is the difference between flat and reducing interest rates? These two types of interest rates differ based on their calculation base: a flat rate uses the original principal, while a reducing rate uses the outstanding balance. What is the difference between nominal and effective interest rates? Nominal is the quoted rate. Comparing types of loans and interest rates requires the effective rate or APR, as these reflect the compounding and charges. Which type of loan has the highest interest rate? Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Summary A loan repayment schedule is a detailed timetable indicating how and when you must repay the borrowed money. It lists the due dates and payment amounts, and breaks down the principal and interest for each payment. It also mentions the remaining loan amount after you make your payment. After referring to the payment schedule, you can plan your monthly budget and see how much total interest you will pay over time. The schedule also helps you stay on track to avoid late fees. A loan repayment schedule provides a structured plan outlining how you will repay the borrowedamount over a specific period. When a lender approves a loan, it provides a loan repayment schedule, listing every Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) you need to pay over the loan tenure. The schedule shows both the principal and interest component. This guide explains what a loan repayment schedule is, what it includes, how it is calculated, and how you can use it to manage your loan effectively. What is a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule, or a payment schedule, meaning the document lenders provide when your loan is approved is a table with all the necessary loan repayment details. It clearly shows every EMI from start to finish, the interest charged, how much you still owe, and when your loan will be fully repaid. It makes financial planning much easier and saves you from surprises later. What does a loan repayment schedule contain? The components of a loan repayment schedule are as follows: Component Meaning EMI number The sequence of each monthly payment. EMI due date The date on which you need to pay EMI. EMI amount The total amount you pay every month. Principal component The portion of the EMI that reduces your loan amount. Interest component The portion of the EMI charged as interest by the lender. Outstanding principal balance The remaining loan amount after each EMI is paid. In a standard reducing-balance loan, the interest component is higher in the initial EMIs because it is calculated on a larger outstanding principal. As you repay the loan, the principal balance decreases, so the interest portion reduces while the principal component gradually increases. How is a loan repayment schedule calculated? To calculate the loan repayment schedule, most lenders use the reducing-balance (amortization) method. Here, monthly interest is calculated on the outstanding principal, and the remaining portion of the EMI is applied to reduce the principal. Since the outstanding balance decreases with each payment, the interest charged on the next EMI is lower. To calculate EMI, you can use the formula given below: EMI = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1) Where, P = principal loan amount r = monthly interest rate n = loan tenure (in months) Here’s an illustrative example for better understanding. Suppose you borrow Rs. 5 lakh for 5 years at an interest rate of 10% per annum. You will have a fixed EMI of Rs. 10,624, and a total interest payout of Rs. 1,37,411. The first few EMIs will contain more interest than principal. Gradually, the interest portion will decrease while the principal repayment will increase. You can use an online EMI calculator to instantly generate a detailed payment schedule. Also Read – Loan vs. Advance What is the importance of a loan repayment schedule? A loan repayment schedule is important for several reasons, such as: Planning your budget: You can track EMI amounts and due dates. Knowing your interest cost: It shows the total interest payable over the loan tenure. Deciding on prepayments: You can estimate potential interest savings. Planning taxes: It helps you keep track of eligible tax benefits on the loan. Comparing loans: You can evaluate different loan offers based on the total repayment cost. How to get your loan repayment schedule? Your lender usually provides a loan repayment schedule when the loan is disbursed. You can also download it at any time through your online loan account or customer portal. If you are planning a new loan, use Tata Capital’s EMI Calculator to estimate your repayment schedule and manage your loan with confidence. What are the tips to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively? If you want to manage your loan repayment schedule effectively, here are some helpful tips: Set up auto-debit: Enable NACH or auto-debit to avoid missing EMI payments. Check before prepaying: Review your schedule to estimate possible interest savings. Request an updated schedule: Ask your lender for a revised schedule if your floating interest rate changes. Track principal repayments: Keep a record of the principal repaid each year for home loan tax filing purposes. Also Read – What is Part-Payment, Pre-Payment, Pre-Closure of Loan? Conclusion A loan repayment schedule is an important financial planning tool that shows how each EMI is divided between principal and interest. It helps you manage your cash flow and make informed prepayment decisions. The actual repayment schedule depends on your loan amount, interest rate, and tenure, and thus, do not refer to the standard ones available online. A loan repayment schedule is a table that includes the EMI amount, payment dates, principal repaid, interest charged, and the remaining loan balance after each payment. How is a loan repayment schedule calculated? A loan repayment schedule is calculated using the loan amount, interest rate, loan tenure, and EMI amount. It shows how every EMI is split between principal and interest until the loan is fully repaid. What is the difference between the principal and interest component in an EMI? The principal is the original loan amount you borrow, while the interest is the cost of borrowing that money. Can I get my loan repayment schedule online? Yes. Most banks and lenders allow you to download your loan repayment schedule through their website, mobile app, or internet banking portal. Does a repayment schedule change on a floating rate loan? Yes. without pledging property or other security. Loans up to ₹7.5 lakh may qualify under government-backed schemes, while higher amounts depend on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant profile. For abroad studies, unsecured options may also be available through some lenders for eligible students. A student who wants to study abroad may be able to obtain an education loan without collateral, depending on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant’s financial profile. There is no need to pledge property, a fixed deposit, or another asset to obtain an education loan. In India, government-backed credit guarantee schemes can cover eligible education loans up to ₹7.5 lakh without collateral or a third-party guarantee. Higher collateral-free financing may also be available depending on the lender, institution, course and co-applicant’s financial profile. What is a Collateral-Free Education Loan? A study loan without collateral is for higher education and does not require you to pledge property, a fixed deposit, or any other asset as security. The lender will assess other factors such as the student’s course, institution, and co-applicant’s income and credit history. Government-backed credit guarantee assistance is also available for eligible loans up to ₹7.5 lakh under CGFSEL. The ₹7.5 Lakh Rule: Where Collateral-Free Is Guaranteed With the IBA Model Education Loan Scheme, education loans may be approved without the need for collateral or a third-party guarantee. The Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Education Loans (CGFSEL), managed by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC), offers a government-backed credit guarantee covering eligible assistance up to ₹7.5 lakh. The scheme guarantees payment against default to the lending institution, so it reduces the lender’s credit risk but does not mean that every applicant is automatically approved for a loan. Note that the ₹7.5 lakh represents the collateral-free limit within the CGFSEL framework. In the case of loans that are covered by the scheme, the borrower is not required to offer property, a fixed deposit, or some other asset as security. The scheme may be relevant when applying through banks under the IBA framework. Here is how the ₹7.5 lakh limit of the non-collateral education loan works: Loan amount Collateral/guarantee requirement Margin under the IBA Model Scheme Up to ₹4 lakh No collateral security or third-party guarantee Nil Above ₹4 lakh up to ₹7.5 lakh No collateral security or third-party guarantee under CGFSEL Around 5% for studies in India and around 15% for studies abroad Note: The CGFSEL guarantee is subject to the scheme’s eligibility conditions and applies through participating lending institutions. If a borrower has a grievance regarding CGFSEL, NCGTC provides a grievance mechanism where the borrower can select the scheme and bank and submit complaint details. NCGTC also provides a dedicated email address and contact number for CGFEL grievances and queries. Collateral-Free Education Loans for Studying Abroad It can be harder to obtain a collateral free education loan for abroad because overseas education can cost ₹25 lakh to ₹80 lakh or more. The CGFSEL framework covers eligible assistance up to ₹7.5 lakh, so larger funding requirements generally depend on lender-specific unsecured products. So, to secure larger funding amounts over 7.5 lakhs, you may have three options. Premier-institution unsecured loans Some banks offer higher-value student loans without collateral to students enrolled in premier institutions or universities. Depending on the lender, institution, course, and the applicant’s and co-applicant’s eligibility, collateral-free loan amounts may range from ₹50 lakh to up to ₹1 crore. Higher overall loan limits may be available, but these may require collateral. NBFC/fintech education loans Specialised education loan providers such as Credila, Avanse and Propelld provide unsecured funding to eligible students. While these no collateral education loans can be more flexible and may be processed more quickly, they may be available at higher interest costs than secured education loans. Tata Capital also provides collateral-free education loans for eligible domestic and overseas education requirements, with options up to ₹85 lakh, subject to eligibility criteria. PM-Vidyalaxmi PM-Vidyalaxmi scheme offers education loans without requiring any collateral or a guarantor to students admitted on merit to eligible Quality Higher Education Institutions (QHEIs) in India. The scheme covers 902 QHEIs. It does not provide funding for a foreign university simply because the student is studying abroad. Lenders may assess the university’s rank and reputation, the employability of the course, the country, the applicant’s academic record, the co-applicant’s income, credit history, and repayment ability before approving your loan application. A lower-ranked university with weak employment prospects may not be eligible for unsecured financing even if the student has an admission offer. So, before applying for the collateral free education loan, you should look at the approved-institution list, maximum unsecured limit, interest rate, and co-applicant requirements rather than assuming that every overseas admission qualifies. Government Schemes That Help (CGFSEL, PM-Vidyalaxmi, CSIS) Before applying for a commercial education loan without security, check whether you are eligible for a government-backed programme because such schemes may eliminate the need for security or reduce the interest rate. The rules and the income limits may change, so it is important to verify the most up-to-date requirements before applying for a non-collateral education loan. The students whose annual family income is up to ₹8 lakh may receive a 3% interest subsidy during the moratorium period on the eligible education-loan amount of up to ₹10 lakh. PM-USP CSIS 100% interest subsidy during the moratorium period on eligible education loans up to ₹10 lakh EWS students with annual family income up to ₹4.5 lakh pursuing eligible technical or professional courses Dr Ambedkar Scheme Interest subsidy on eligible education loans during the moratorium period Eligible OBC and EBC students pursuing approved Master’s, M.Phil or PhD courses abroad, subject to the scheme’s income, admission and loan conditions Before choosing a commercial study loan without collateral, ensure you look at all the relevant schemes. For information on education loans and the schemes, you can use the Vidya Lakshmi portal and the official PM-Vidyalaxmi information provided by the Ministry of Education. Eligibility and Documents Obtaining a non-collateral education loan involves more than submitting the admission letter. Because no property or other asset is pledged, lenders check the academic record, course, university, and the financial strength of your co-applicant. Key eligibility factors Key requirements to become eligible for a loan include: Confirmed Admission: You should have the admission letter from an eligible or approved institution. Course: Lenders prefer courses that have good career and employment prospects. STEM and other career-focused programmes may get closer consideration. Co-applicant income and credit score: Lenders may assess important factors such as the co-applicant’s income, CIBIL score , employment stability, and existing financial obligations to approve your collateral-free education loan for abroad. Academic record: Marks obtained in Class 10, 12, and at graduation can strengthen your education loan application. Tata Capital’s eligibility criteria include a minimum academic qualification of 60%, subject to the applicable product terms. Visa and admission proof: Admission letter and visa documents are necessary while applying for an education loan. Documents Required The essential documents for a education loan collateral free are: Admission letter Academic marksheets and certificates ID and address proof Co-applicant’s income documents and other KYC documents Course fee structure Interest Rates, Moratorium and the Real Cost An unsecured education loan for abroad may have a higher interest rate than a secured loan because no property or other asset is pledged. Tata Capital currently offers education loan rates ranging from 9.50% to 21%. The exact rate is determined according to the borrower and the loan terms. Interest generally continues to accrue during the moratorium period. If the borrower does not service the interest during this period, the unpaid interest may be capitalised and increase the outstanding loan balance, subject to the applicable loan terms and scheme conditions. For example, on a loan of ₹20 lakh at a rate of 10.5%, the interest amounts to approximately ₹2.1 lakh over one year. If unpaid interest is capitalised, this can increase the outstanding balance and the eventual repayment cost. So, if possible, the interest should be paid during the moratorium period to keep the final loan cost lower. When applying for a collateral-free education loan abroad, you should compare the interest rate, processing fees, moratorium terms, repayment period, and the total amount to be repaid. You should also look at the lender’s Key Facts Statement (KFS), because it provides important information regarding the loan’s annualised cost and charges. Tax Benefit: Section 80E A study loan without collateral can also provide a tax advantage. According to Section 80E , the interest paid on an eligible education loan may be deducted from taxable income. There is no monetary limit on the eligible interest deduction, subject to the conditions of Section 80E, and the deduction can be claimed for up to eight assessment years. The deduction is available on the interest paid, not the principal repayment. It applies to both secured and unsecured education loans that meet the requirements of Section 80E. The person who obtains the loan and pays interest can claim the deduction. A parent who takes a loan for their children can also claim a deduction, subject to the applicable conditions. Because the tax rules can change, it is suggested to check the latest Income Tax Department provisions or consult a qualified tax professional before claiming the deduction. How to Apply for a Collateral-Free Education Loan If you are wondering how to get an education loan without collateral, follow these steps: Step 1: Check government schemes eligibility: Before applying for a collateral-free education loan abroad, check applicable government schemes and eligibility because these may reduce the borrowing cost. Step 2:Compare lenders: Compare the interest rates, maximum collateral-free amount, processing fees, moratorium period, and the repayment terms. Do not simply choose the loan with the lower interest rate. Step 3: Keep your documents ready: Keep your admission letter, school records, KYC papers, course fee details, and the co-applicant’s income and financial documents ready. Step 4: Apply with the lender: You can compare the available options and apply via the lender’s official website. Tata Capital Education Loan is an option you can consider to get a student loan without collateral. Step 5: Complete verification: The lender verifies the information and documents submitted with the application and assesses your eligibility under its lending criteria. Step 6: Review the sanction and disbursal: Once the loan has been approved, ensure you carefully check the approved amount, the interest rate, the fees, the moratorium, and the repayment terms. Once the necessary formalities have been completed, the loan will be disbursed to the institution’s fees. Conclusion An education loan without collateral may be used to pay for higher education without putting your property up as security. Eligible loans up to ₹7.5 lakh may receive government-backed guarantee support without collateral, whereas larger amounts depend on the lender, institution, course, and co-applicant’s profile. When considering studies abroad, you should carefully compare unsecured loans and check the government schemes before borrowing a loan. Also consider the interest that can accrue during the moratorium and whether you qualify for the Section 80E deduction. Tata Capital is one option to compare eligible students looking for collateral-free education financing. Disclaimer: This information is for general awareness only. Scheme limits, interest rates, eligibility criteria, and lender terms may change. Always verify the latest terms with the relevant government authority or lender before applying. For unsecured loans, lenders may assess the co-applicant's income, credit record, employment and repayment ability as part of the application. Are collateral-free education loan interest rates higher? They can be. Because no asset is used as security, an unsecured loan carries a higher credit risk to the lender. NBFCs and authorised platforms using Aadhaar or other verified personal details. Identity verification is still required, and a no-PAN check may not capture your complete credit history. If your PAN is available, using it can help match your credit accounts more accurately You can check CIBIL score without PAN card using Aadhaar, your name, date of birth and registered mobile number, or through your bank/NBFC app, depending on the platform. However, you will still need to verify your identity, usually through an OTP or another authentication method. A no-PAN check may not show your complete credit history because credit accounts are commonly linked to your PAN. Websites promising a “no PAN, no OTP” CIBIL check should be treated as unsafe. This article explains the legitimate ways to check your CIBIL score without a PAN card, why identity verification is still required, how to check your score using PAN when it is available, and what to look for when avoiding fraudulent credit-score websites. Can You Really Check a CIBIL Score Without a PAN Card? Yes. The available method depends on the platform. However, PAN does remain an important identifier because lenders commonly report it with your loan and credit card information. It therefore helps the credit bureau match different credit accounts to the correct person. Without a valid PAN, the platform may still identify you through other information, but some accounts may not be matched. Make sure to check which ID options the platform accepts before starting. Ways to Check Your CIBIL Score Without a PAN Card You can check your CIBIL score without a PAN card through certain banks, NBFCs and authorised platforms using Aadhaar, another accepted ID or verified personal details. 1. Through Your Bank or NBFC App Some banks and NBFCs provide a credit score or credit-health feature within their app or internet banking service. To check: Log in through the official app or website. Look for the credit score or credit health section. Follow the instructions shown on screen. Complete any additional authentication requested. View your available score. If you are already verified within the app, the provider may not ask for PAN or a fresh OTP again. The process varies by provider. 2. Using Aadhaar or Another Accepted ID Some authorised financial platforms may allow Aadhaar or another accepted identity document to verify you. The process may involve: Selecting the available ID type. Entering the corresponding ID number. Providing your name, date of birth and contact details. Completing OTP or another required authentication step. Viewing the score if the platform can match your credit profile.. 3. Using Your Name, Date of Birth and Mobile Number Some platforms may first try to locate your credit profile using details such as your full name, date of birth and mobile number. This route still requires identity verification and may not retrieve every PAN-linked account. The platform may ask for an accepted ID or PAN if it cannot establish an accurate match. If you have access to your PAN, using it can make it easier to match the credit accounts reported against your profile. Why You Usually Still Need OTP (and Why That’s a Good Thing) You usually need an OTP because your identity must be verified before your CIBIL information can be released. This protects you from someone using your PAN or other personal details to access your credit report without your permission. A legitimate consumer service cannot give you your CIBIL score with no identity verification at all. If you search for checking CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP, be cautious of websites promising a “PAN only, no OTP” check. A request for your PAN alone should not be enough to access your credit information. OTP is a security measure and not an unnecessary friction. It helps confirm that you are the person requesting access to your credit information. You may not always receive a fresh OTP if you have already been authenticated through your bank or financial app, but some form of identity verification is still required. If a website promises to show your CIBIL score without OTP or any other verification, treat it as a red flag and avoid sharing your personal or financial information. How to Spot Fake ‘Free CIBIL Check’ Websites You can spot a fake CIBIL check website by checking whether it uses proper identity verification, protects your financial information and clearly explains how it handles your data. A legitimate check may ask for your PAN or another accepted ID, mobile number and OTP or another form of identity verification. Warning signs include: No identity verification: Be cautious if a site promises your credit report without verifying who you are. Requests for banking credentials: A credit score check should not require your debit or credit card PIN, CVV, UPI PIN or net-banking password. Requests to share an OTP: Never tell an OTP to someone over a call, email or message. Suspicious website addresses: Check for spelling changes or domains designed to resemble a recognised financial institution. No clear privacy information: Avoid sites that do not explain how they collect and use your personal information. Misleading payment requests: CIBIL currently provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year. Note : If you become a victim of financial cyber fraud, report it through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal or call 1930. Checking Your CIBIL Score With a PAN Card (The Standard Way) If you have your PAN, it can make it easier to match the credit accounts reported under your name. To check your CIBIL score by PAN card, you can: Visit the official CIBIL platform or an authorised provider. Choose the option for a CIBIL Score and Report. Enter your PAN, name, date of birth and mobile number. Complete the required OTP or other identity verification. View your available score and credit report. Make sure the details you enter match your official records so the correct credit profile can be identified. Under RBI rules, you are entitled to one free full credit report, including your credit score, in a calendar year after due authentication. CIBIL also provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year, while banks, NBFCs and other authorised platforms may offer free periodic checks depending on their current services. Also Read – What is the maximum CIBIL score What You’ll Need and What It Means for Your Score To check your CIBIL score, you generally need an accepted ID such as PAN or Aadhaar, your registered mobile number for authentication, and basic personal details such as your name and date of birth. You may also need: Email address, if required by the platform Access to the required authentication method, such as OTP Since it is a self-check and not a lender enquiry made when you apply for credit, checking your own CIBIL score causes zero impact on your score. Understanding the CIBIL score range can help you analyse what each number indicates. If you check your score without PAN and an account appears to be missing, cross-check your credit report using PAN when it is available. A PAN-based check may help match accounts that were not identified through the no-PAN route. Also Read – Will a Loan Settlement Ruin My CIBIL Score Conclusion You can check your CIBIL score without a PAN card through NBFCs or authorised platforms using Aadhaar, another accepted ID or verified personal details. However, identity verification is still required, and a no-PAN check may not always show your complete credit history. If you have your PAN, using it can make it easier to match your credit accounts. Avoid unfamiliar websites promising to check CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP and no other verification. Once you know your score, you can check your eligibility and applicable terms for a Tata Capital Personal Loan through the Tata Capital website or app. Disclaimer : This article provides general information only. Credit scores and reports are issued by TransUnion CIBIL. Processes and availability may change, so use only official or authorised channels. If you suspect financial cyber fraud, report it through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. FAQs Can I check my CIBIL score without a PAN card? Yes. If you want to know how to check CIBIL score without a PAN card, some platforms may accept Aadhaar, another permitted ID or verified personal details. Your bank or NBFC may also provide access to your credit score, depending on the service available and the verification process it follows. Can I check my CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP? No. You will still need to verify your identity. If you are already logged in to your bank or financial app, a separate OTP may not be needed. Be careful with websites that say you can check CIBIL score by PAN card without OTP or any verification. How do I check my CIBIL score with my PAN card? To check CIBIL score by PAN card, use the official CIBIL platform or an authorised provider. Enter your PAN, name, date of birth and contact details, then complete the required verification. When you check CIBIL score using a PAN card, make sure the information matches your official records so the correct credit profile can be identified. Is it safe to check my CIBIL score on third-party websites? Yes, but only if the platform is recognised and follows proper security and authentication practices. Avoid websites asking for your card PIN, CVV, UPI PIN or net-banking password. Also check whether the site clearly explains how it uses your data and whether it requires proper identity verification before showing your credit information. Does checking my own CIBIL score lower it? No. Checking your own CIBIL score does not lower it. It is treated as a self-check rather than a lender enquiry made for a new credit application. Will a check without PAN show my full credit history? Not always. Some accounts may not show up without your PAN. If your report looks incomplete, check it again using your PAN when possible. How often can I check my CIBIL score for free? CIBIL currently provides one free CIBIL Score and Report once a year. RBI rules also provide for one free full credit report, including the credit score, in each calendar year after due authentication. Additional checks may be available through banks, NBFCs or authorised platforms, depending on their current service and access policy. Insurance Medical Insurance Other Insurance Wellness solutions Home Insurance Travel Insurance Investment Mutual Fund Summary: Retirement planning starts with estimating the retirement corpus you will need to maintain your desired lifestyle after you stop working. Your age, income, risk appetite, liquidity needs and tax situation can then help determine how NPS, EPF, PPF, mutual funds and pension plans fit into your retirement strategy. Looking for the best retirement plan in India starts with the amount you may need after retirement rather than a product name. A pension plan, NPS, EPF, PPF or mutual fund can each play a different role depending on your age, income, risk appetite and need for liquidity. In fact, your tax regime also affects which options may suit you. For income earned from 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies and the new tax regime remains the default, although taxpayers can opt for the old regime where permitted. Employer contributions to NPS remain an important exception. The same option can therefore work differently for two people with similar retirement goals. Your corpus target, time to retirement, ability to take risk and need for access to the money should determine how you combine the available options. This guide compares the main retirement-planning categories rather than ranking individual branded products as the “best” choice. How Much Do You Need to Retire? First estimate how much annual income you may need after retirement. Start with your current household expenses, remove costs that may end before retirement and add expenses that could rise later, particularly healthcare. Then account for inflation until your expected retirement age. For example, suppose your household expenses are ₹6 lakh a year today and you plan to retire in 20 years. At an assumed inflation rate of 6% a year, the same level of spending would be about ₹19.2 lakh annually by then. Next, estimate how long the corpus may need to last and factor in any pension, rent or other regular income you expect to receive. A retirement calculator can combine your age, existing savings, expected expenses, inflation and return assumptions to estimate the gap. Once you know the target corpus and any shortfall, you can decide how to allocate your retirement savings across pension schemes, provident funds and market-linked investments. Main Retirement Planning Options in India To begin with the major options, note that NPS, PPF, mutual funds , EPF, annuities and SCSS do not serve the same purpose. Their risk, liquidity, tax treatment and income structure are different. NPS and mutual funds are market-linked, while EPF, PPF and SCSS follow different government-backed structures. Insurer pension products may provide more predictable income but can offer less flexibility. These differences matter more than choosing a product simply because it is presented as the best pension plan in India. Option What it is Risk/return Lock-in and liquidity New-regime tax position May suit NPS Retirement savings account regulated by PFRDA Returns move with the market Withdrawals are allowed only as per NPS rules Personal NPS deductions do not generally apply under the new regime, though eligible employer contributions can still get a deduction People who want to build retirement EPF Employment-linked provident fund funded by employee and employer contributions Interest declared under the EPF framework; government-backed retirement savings structure Withdrawals subject to EPF rules Employee contribution deduction generally unavailable under the new regime Eligible salaried employees PPF Government-backed long-term savings scheme Government-declared interest 15-year maturity, with limited access before maturity Contribution deduction generally unavailable under the new regime; interest and qualifying maturity proceeds retain separate tax treatment Those prioritising capital protection Mutual funds Market-linked funds investing in equity, debt or a combination Returns depend on market performance Most are comparatively liquid; ELSS has a lock-in No ELSS deduction under the new regime; capital-gains tax depends on fund type Investors seeking growth and flexibility Annuity/insurance pension plans Insurance arrangements designed to provide retirement income May offer guaranteed income according to policy terms Liquidity and surrender terms vary Personal deductions depend on the applicable tax regime and product Those prioritising predictable income SCSS Government-backed savings scheme for eligible senior citizens Government-declared interest Subject to scheme tenure and premature-withdrawal rules Interest is taxable; old-regime deduction rules differ from new-regime treatment Eligible retirees seeking regular income Tax and scheme information below is based on rules available in August 2026 and may change. Retirement Planning and the New Tax Regime: What Changed For Tax Year 2026-27, which covers income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies. The new tax regime continues as the default regime, while taxpayers who are eligible can opt for the old regime. Under the new regime, many personal deductions that influenced retirement-product choices under the old regime are no longer available. The deduction corresponding to the old Section 80C is now provided under Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The ₹1.5 lakh aggregate deduction remains in the new Act, but Section 123 is not available under the new concessional tax regime . Retirement-related provision Old regime New regime Eligible PPF, EPF, ELSS and qualifying retirement contributions Deduction may apply within prescribed limits Personal deduction generally unavailable Personal NPS contribution Applicable deductions may be claimed subject to conditions Personal deduction generally unavailable Additional NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(1B) Deduction available up to ₹50,000, subject to conditions Not available Employer NPS contribution Deduction available subject to applicable limits Continues to qualify subject to applicable limits Standard deduction for eligible salary/pension income Available as applicable Available under current rules Maturity or withdrawal proceeds Depends on instrument Separate exemption or tax rules may still apply The Income Tax Department confirms that 80CCD(1B) cannot be claimed under the new regime. Under the old framework, the additional deduction was capped at ₹50,000. For employer NPS contributions, the applicable deduction limit depends on the employer category and the governing conditions. The current Income Tax Department guidance lists 14% for Central or State Government employers and 10% for PSU or other employers. Additionally, do not choose a pension plan mainly for a tax break. Check whether the deduction applies under your regime, then compare risk, liquidity, charges, payout structure and withdrawal terms. Note : The old Section 80C reference should be used only when discussing the old Act. For income earned from 1 April 2026 onwards, refer to Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Also read – ELSS Mutual Funds NPS, EPF and PPF: The Building Blocks NPS, EPF and PPF are commonly used for long-term retirement savings, but they work in different ways. NPS : NPS (National Pension System) is a market-linked pension scheme in India regulated by PFRDA. Contributions can be allocated across permitted asset classes and returns depend on the performance of the underlying investments. Under the current PFRDA framework for the All Citizen Model, a normal exit can allow up to 80% of the accumulated corpus as a lump sum, with at least 20% used to purchase an annuity, subject to applicable conditions and corpus thresholds. This 80/20 structure applies to the current All Citizen Model, so it should not be replaced with the older 60/40 figure without specifying the NPS model. The withdrawal limit and tax exemption are not the same. Current income-tax rules provide exemption for up to 60% of the NPS corpus on final lump-sum withdrawal, while pension received from an annuity is taxable. EPF : Employee Provident Fund (EPF) is employment-linked and receives employee and employer contributions. Subject to applicable conditions, EPF generally follows an EEE structure, meaning qualifying contributions, interest and withdrawals receive tax benefits. PPF : Public Provident Fund (PPF) is government-backed with a 15-year term. Interest and qualifying maturity proceeds are tax-free, while its contribution deduction mainly benefits old-regime taxpayers. Annuity and Pension Plans from Insurers: How to Evaluate Them An insurance pension plan usually involves paying premiums over time or investing a lump sum to receive retirement income later. An immediate annuity starts payouts soon after purchase, while a deferred arrangement begins at a future date. The pension amount alone does not tell you whether an annuity is suitable. Check for: Annuity Rate: Compare the income offered against the amount invested. Payout Structure: Check whether payments continue for one life, joint lives or include return of purchase price. Charges: Review costs that may apply during accumulation, withdrawal or surrender. Liquidity: Check whether and when the invested amount can be accessed. Inflation Impact: A fixed pension can lose purchasing power over a long retirement. Insurer Record: Review relevant financial strength, servicing and claims information. Tax Treatment: Check how contributions, maturity proceeds and pension income are taxed. Annuity rates can be modest compared with the growth potential of market-linked assets over long periods and surrender terms can be restrictive. The trade-off is greater certainty of income when comparing pension plans in India. Also read – What is Net Asset Value How to Build Your Retirement Plan: A Simple Framework A retirement corpus is usually built from more than one source. The mix can be planned around 5 factors: Define the Corpus Goal: Estimate future living, healthcare and other retirement costs after inflation, then calculate how much you may need to accumulate. Use Different Options for Different Needs: EPF or PPF may add stability, mutual funds can provide market-linked growth, NPS can bring structure to retirement investing and an annuity may help create predictable income. Check Your Tax Regime: Do not assume an investment carries the same deduction under both regimes. If your employer contributes to NPS, check whether the available deduction applies to you. Increase Contributions as Income Grows: A contribution fixed early in your career may become too small as income and expenses rise. Increasing it periodically can help keep the corpus target within reach. Review the Plan Regularly: Recalculate the requirement when your income, expenses, retirement age, investment performance or tax rules change. When comparing the best retirement plans, assess the overall mix against your time horizon, risk capacity, liquidity requirements and expected retirement income. For individual investment decisions, consider consulting a SEBI-registered investment adviser. Common Retirement Planning Mistakes Retirement plans often fall short because people start late, underestimate future costs or rely too heavily on one investment. Common mistakes include: Buying Mainly for a Tax Deduction: A deduction available under the old regime may not apply under the new regime. Depending on One Instrument: A single option may not provide enough growth, liquidity and income flexibility. Ignoring Inflation: The amount needed to maintain today’s lifestyle can rise considerably by retirement. Starting Too Late: A shorter accumulation period can require substantially higher contributions. Underestimating Healthcare Costs: Medical spending can become a larger part of the household budget later in life. Ignoring NPS Annuity Taxation: Pension received from the annuity portion is taxable under current rules. Not Reviewing the Plan: Tax rules, pension regulations and personal circumstances can change. Also read – What is the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)? Conclusion A retirement plan should show how much money you need, where that money will come from and how each investment supports that goal. NPS can add market-linked retirement savings, EPF and PPF can provide stability, mutual funds can support long-term growth and annuities can create regular income after retirement. The mix should be reviewed as your income, expenses, retirement age or tax position changes. That is more useful than choosing a product mainly for a deduction or advertised return. There is no single best retirement plan in India for everyone. The suitable mix depends on your retirement corpus, age, income, risk tolerance, liquidity needs and tax regime. The right choice depends on how much growth, stability, liquidity and retirement income you need. What is the difference between a pension plan and NPS? A pension plan from an insurer generally provides retirement benefits or annuity income according to its policy terms. NPS is a PFRDA-regulated and a market-linked retirement system. They differ in investment structure, liquidity, charges, exit rules, tax treatment and the way retirement income is generated. Do pension plans still give a tax benefit under the new regime? Not necessarily. Many personal deductions associated with retirement investments are not available under the new regime. Eligible employer NPS contributions remain an important exception. Check the current tax treatment of the specific investment rather than assuming a pension product automatically provides a deduction. How much should I invest for retirement in India? There is no fixed amount or percentage for everyone. Estimate your future expenses after inflation, calculate the corpus required and subtract existing retirement savings and expected income. Your age, years until retirement, risk level and expected investment performance will influence the contribution required. What are the government pension schemes in India? NPS is a major government-regulated pension scheme in India. Other retirement-related arrangements include the Atal Pension Yojana and, for eligible government employees, the Unified Pension Scheme. EPF, PPF and SCSS are also widely used for retirement savings, although they do not all operate as pension schemes in the same way. Is NPS better than an insurance pension plan? Not necessarily. NPS is market-linked, while an insurance pension plan may offer guaranteed or defined income depending on the policy. The better option depends on whether you prioritise growth potential, predictable income, access to your money and the costs involved. When should I start retirement planning Start earlier as it gives your contributions more time to compound. If you begin later, the amount required each month may be higher to reach the same corpus. At any age, start by calculating the gap between your existing retirement savings and the amount you expect to need. need to maintain your desired lifestyle after you stop working. Your age, income, risk appetite, liquidity needs and tax situation can then help determine how NPS, EPF, PPF, mutual funds and pension plans fit into your retirement strategy. Looking for the best retirement plan in India starts with the amount you may need after retirement rather than a product name. A pension plan, NPS, EPF, PPF or mutual fund can each play a different role depending on your age, income, risk appetite and need for liquidity. In fact, your tax regime also affects which options may suit you. For income earned from 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies and the new tax regime remains the default, although taxpayers can opt for the old regime where permitted. Employer contributions to NPS remain an important exception. The same option can therefore work differently for two people with similar retirement goals. Your corpus target, time to retirement, ability to take risk and need for access to the money should determine how you combine the available options. This guide compares the main retirement-planning categories rather than ranking individual branded products as the “best” choice. How Much Do You Need to Retire? First estimate how much annual income you may need after retirement. Start with your current household expenses, remove costs that may end before retirement and add expenses that could rise later, particularly healthcare. Then account for inflation until your expected retirement age. For example, suppose your household expenses are ₹6 lakh a year today and you plan to retire in 20 years. At an assumed inflation rate of 6% a year, the same level of spending would be about ₹19.2 lakh annually by then. Next, estimate how long the corpus may need to last and factor in any pension, rent or other regular income you expect to receive. A retirement calculator can combine your age, existing savings, expected expenses, inflation and return assumptions to estimate the gap. Once you know the target corpus and any shortfall, you can decide how to allocate your retirement savings across pension schemes, provident funds and market-linked investments. Main Retirement Planning Options in India To begin with the major options, note that NPS, PPF, mutual funds , EPF, annuities and SCSS do not serve the same purpose. Their risk, liquidity, tax treatment and income structure are different. NPS and mutual funds are market-linked, while EPF, PPF and SCSS follow different government-backed structures. Insurer pension products may provide more predictable income but can offer less flexibility. These differences matter more than choosing a product simply because it is presented as the best pension plan in India. Retirement Planning and the New Tax Regime: What Changed For Tax Year 2026-27, which covers income earned from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, the Income-tax Act, 2025 applies. The new tax regime continues as the default regime, while taxpayers who are eligible can opt for the old regime. Under the new regime, many personal deductions that influenced retirement-product choices under the old regime are no longer available. The deduction corresponding to the old Section 80C is now provided under Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. The ₹1.5 lakh aggregate deduction remains in the new Act, but Section 123 is not available under the new concessional tax regime . Under the old framework, the additional deduction was capped at ₹50,000. For employer NPS contributions, the applicable deduction limit depends on the employer category and the governing conditions. The current Income Tax Department guidance lists 14% for Central or State Government employers and 10% for PSU or other employers. Additionally, do not choose a pension plan mainly for a tax break. Check whether the deduction applies under your regime, then compare risk, liquidity, charges, payout structure and withdrawal terms. Note : The old Section 80C reference should be used only when discussing the old Act. For income earned from 1 April 2026 onwards, refer to Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025. NPS : NPS (National Pension System) is a market-linked pension scheme in India regulated by PFRDA. Contributions can be allocated across permitted asset classes and returns depend on the performance of the underlying investments. Under the current PFRDA framework for the All Citizen Model, a normal exit can allow up to 80% of the accumulated corpus as a lump sum, with at least 20% used to purchase an annuity, subject to applicable conditions and corpus thresholds. This 80/20 structure applies to the current All Citizen Model, so it should not be replaced with the older 60/40 figure without specifying the NPS model. The withdrawal limit and tax exemption are not the same. Current income-tax rules provide exemption for up to 60% of the NPS corpus on final lump-sum withdrawal, while pension received from an annuity is taxable. EPF : Employee Provident Fund (EPF) is employment-linked and receives employee and employer contributions. Subject to applicable conditions, EPF generally follows an EEE structure, meaning qualifying contributions, interest and withdrawals receive tax benefits. PPF : Public Provident Fund (PPF) is government-backed with a 15-year term. Interest and qualifying maturity proceeds are tax-free, while its contribution deduction mainly benefits old-regime taxpayers. Annuity and Pension Plans from Insurers: How to Evaluate Them An insurance pension plan usually involves paying premiums over time or investing a lump sum to receive retirement income later. An immediate annuity starts payouts soon after purchase, while a deferred arrangement begins at a future date. The pension amount alone does not tell you whether an annuity is suitable. Check for: Annuity Rate: Compare the income offered against the amount invested. Payout Structure: Check whether payments continue for one life, joint lives or include return of purchase price. Charges: Review costs that may apply during accumulation, withdrawal or surrender. Liquidity: Check whether and when the invested amount can be accessed. Inflation Impact: A fixed pension can lose purchasing power over a long retirement. Insurer Record: Review relevant financial strength, servicing and claims information. Tax Treatment: Check how contributions, maturity proceeds and pension income are taxed. Annuity rates can be modest compared with the growth potential of market-linked assets over long periods and surrender terms can be restrictive. The trade-off is greater certainty of income when comparing pension plans in India. Also read – What is Net Asset Value How to Build Your Retirement Plan: A Simple Framework A retirement corpus is usually built from more than one source. The mix can be planned around 5 factors: Define the Corpus Goal: Estimate future living, healthcare and other retirement costs after inflation, then calculate how much you may need to accumulate. Use Different Options for Different Needs: EPF or PPF may add stability, mutual funds can provide market-linked growth, NPS can bring structure to retirement investing and an annuity may help create predictable income. Check Your Tax Regime: Do not assume an investment carries the same deduction under both regimes. If your employer contributes to NPS, check whether the available deduction applies to you. Increase Contributions as Income Grows: A contribution fixed early in your career may become too small as income and expenses rise. Increasing it periodically can help keep the corpus target within reach. Review the Plan Regularly: Recalculate the requirement when your income, expenses, retirement age, investment performance or tax rules change. When comparing the best retirement plans, assess the overall mix against your time horizon, risk capacity, liquidity requirements and expected retirement income. For individual investment decisions, consider consulting a SEBI-registered investment adviser. Common Retirement Planning Mistakes Retirement plans often fall short because people start late, underestimate future costs or rely too heavily on one investment. Common mistakes include: Buying Mainly for a Tax Deduction: A deduction available under the old regime may not apply under the new regime. Depending on One Instrument: A single option may not provide enough growth, liquidity and income flexibility. Ignoring Inflation: The amount needed to maintain today’s lifestyle can rise considerably by retirement. Starting Too Late: A shorter accumulation period can require substantially higher contributions. Underestimating Healthcare Costs: Medical spending can become a larger part of the household budget later in life. Ignoring NPS Annuity Taxation: Pension received from the annuity portion is taxable under current rules. Not Reviewing the Plan: Tax rules, pension regulations and personal circumstances can change. Also read – What is the Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)? Conclusion A retirement plan should show how much money you need, where that money will come from and how each investment supports that goal. NPS can add market-linked retirement savings, EPF and PPF can provide stability, mutual funds can support long-term growth and annuities can create regular income after retirement. The mix should be reviewed as your income, expenses, retirement age or tax position changes. That is more useful than choosing a product mainly for a deduction or advertised return. There is no single best retirement plan in India for everyone. The suitable mix depends on your retirement corpus, age, income, risk tolerance, liquidity needs and tax regime. The right choice depends on how much growth, stability, liquidity and retirement income you need. What is the difference between a pension plan and NPS? A pension plan from an insurer generally provides retirement benefits or annuity income according to its policy terms. NPS is a PFRDA-regulated and a market-linked retirement system. They differ in investment structure, liquidity, charges, exit rules, tax treatment and the way retirement income is generated. Do pension plans still give a tax benefit under the new regime? Not necessarily. Many personal deductions associated with retirement investments are not available under the new regime. Eligible employer NPS contributions remain an important exception. Check the current tax treatment of the specific investment rather than assuming a pension product automatically provides a deduction. How much should I invest for retirement in India? There is no fixed amount or percentage for everyone. Estimate your future expenses after inflation, calculate the corpus required and subtract existing retirement savings and expected income. Your age, years until retirement, risk level and expected investment performance will influence the contribution required. What are the government pension schemes in India? NPS is a major government-regulated pension scheme in India. Other retirement-related arrangements include the Atal Pension Yojana and, for eligible government employees, the Unified Pension Scheme. EPF, PPF and SCSS are also widely used for retirement savings, although they do not all operate as pension schemes in the same way. Is NPS better than an insurance pension plan? Not necessarily. NPS is market-linked, while an insurance pension plan may offer guaranteed or defined income depending on the policy. The better option depends on whether you prioritise growth potential, predictable income, access to your money and the costs involved. When should I start retirement planning Start earlier as it gives your contributions more time to compound. If you begin later, the amount required each month may be higher to reach the same corpus. At any age, start by calculating the gap between your existing retirement savings and the amount you expect to need. more expensive. Education loans come to the rescue for those who want to avoid shelling out the entire cost of education out of pocket. When you apply for an education loan , the lender uses your CIBIL or credit score to determine your creditworthiness. A high CIBIL score ensures the lender that you’re not a credit risk. But what if, as a student, you don’t have a credit score? Is CIBIL score required for an education loan in that case? How much CIBIL score required for education loan? Does education loan affect CIBIL score? Read on to find out. What is the Minimum CIBIL Score Required for Education Loan in India? The minimum credit score required by different lenders varies however, typically the minimum education loan CIBIL score required is 750. If you’re a student without any credit history, then you can apply for an education loan with a working parent as a joint applicant or a guarantor . In such a case, the lender will consider your parents’ credit report to determine their repayment capacity on your behalf. In this case, the following documents are required: Identity Proof, such as an Aadhar card, passport, or other government-issued ID for both the student and the co-applicant. Academic records, including mark sheets and passing certificates from school. Admission letter from the institute you’re planning to attend with fee structure. Income tax returns, salary statements and other financial documents of the co-applicant. Why is CIBIL Score Important for Education Loan Approval? Education loans allow students to study in their desired country and institution, providing support for tuition, lodging, books, and more. CIBIL scores are central to determining whether an education loan is approved. With a higher credit score, you can access the following education loan benefits: Lower interest rates: A good credit score can help you avail of an education loan at lower interest rates , reducing your repayment burden for education loan CIBIL score. Approval for higher loan amounts: A high credit score also elevates your chances of being approved for a higher education loan amount, reducing your financial burden. Possibility of longer loan tenure: A good credit score can also help you become eligible for longer education loan tenures. A longer loan tenure results in smaller EMIs , reducing your immediate financial burden. Faster approval from the lender: With a good credit score over 750, your education loans can get approved faster by the lender, relieving you of any financial uncertainty. To improve your CIBIL score for education loan, follow these steps: Maintain a good credit utilisation ratio: This refers to the total percentage of credit you have used. It is essential to keep it between 30%-50%. Repay all debts : Making timely repayments on loans, bills, and other bowstrings can help improve tour credit score. Time your loan applications: Getting rejected for a loan can cause your CIBIL score to drop. Do not immediately apply for another loan right after being rejected. How to Improve Your CIBIL Score for Education Loan Approval It is crucial to have a good CIBIL score for education loans. Most financial institutions require a minimum CIBIL score for education loans (most set at 750 or higher). However, if you do not have this score, worry not! Below are some ways to improve your CIBIL score: Pay all existing EMIs and credit card bills on time, as payment history heavily impacts your score. Keep credit use low and avoid maxing out the limit on your credit card. If you have multiple loans, try repaying or closing them, especially multiple small loans. Students without a credit history must ensure their co-applicant has a strong CIBIL score and stable income. Regularly go over your credit report for errors and promptly have inaccuracies corrected. How an Education Loan affects your CIBIL Score Just like any other type of loan , an education loan also affects your credit score depending on your repayment behaviour. It is also reflected in your credit history. If you’re regular with your EMI payments and have a clean borrowing history, it will positively reflect in your credit report. The positive effects of an education loan on your CIBIL score include the following: Better Credit Score: If you pay your education loan on time, your credit score improves. This means paying your EMIs on time after the moratorium period without missing. Better Credit Mix: Credit mix means having different types of credits or loans, both secured and unsecured, such as home loans , car loans , education loans, etc. A diverse credit mix boosts your credit score. Building a Long Credit History: Education is usually a long-duration loan. Paying off this loan in earnest builds a long and strong credit history, boosting your credit score. In contrast, repeated delays in EMI repayments can unfavourably affect your credit score. The negative effects of an education loan on your CIBIL score. You can perform a CIBIL score check online to keep track. What to Do If You Have No Credit Score Before Applying for a Student Loan? A CIBIL score is required for education loans, especially when applying to traditional private and public-sector banks. But what do you do when you don’t have a credit score? We outline some ways to apply for an education loan without a CIBIL score: 1. Government-backed schemes The Indian Government supports students from economically weaker sections through schemes such as the Central Sector Interest Subsidy Scheme (CSIS) or the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme. 2. Apply with collateral and co-applicants Many financial institutions will grant students education loans even if they don’t have a CIBIL score, provided they apply with a strong co-applicant or good collateral. This helps lenders to offset risk. 3. Explore NBFCs and alternative lenders Apart from traditional banks, alternative lenders like NBFCs offer competitive education loans, with rates varying by profile. Some may allow you to apply without a CIBIL score as well! Can I Get an Education Loan with Low CIBIL Score in India? Applicants can get an education loan despite having a low CIBIL score in many ways. These include: Having a co-applicant with good income and a high CIBIL score Maintaining a good academic record Getting admission to a reputed course and university, with good employment outcomes Providing strong collateral Applying for government schemes or NBFCs Does Co-Applicant’s CIBIL Score Impact the Education Loan? Yes, the co-applicant’s CIBIL score will impact the education loan. Since most students lack a credit history of their own, financial institutions will look at the co-applicant’s (usually a parent or guardian) credit history and income. A poor CIBIL score could lead to rejection, higher interest rates, and other unfavourable terms. In contrast, a good CIBIL score could lead to better repayment terms and interest rates. Conclusion A good CIBIL score for education loan above 750 provides many benefits when applying for an education loan. If you’re a student, the bank considers the credit score of your parents or guardian. Timely repayment of an education loan affects your credit score positively.
